Absolute Zero? Start Here (Day 0)

Zero experience welcome

Never written a line of code? Perfect — this page is for you. In the next 20 minutes you will create your first web page and understand what HTML, CSS and JavaScript actually are.

Your first web page in 3 steps

Step 1. Open any text editor (Notepad on Windows, TextEdit on Mac — set to plain text) and type this exactly:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>My first page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello, I am learning the web!</h1>
  <p>This page was made by me on day zero.</p>
</body>
</html>

Step 2. Save the file as hello.html (make sure it ends with .html, not .txt).

Step 3. Double-click the file. It opens in your browser. You are now a web developer — everything after this is leveling up.

Pro tip — You just did real web development

That file IS a website: the same HTML professionals write, opened the same way (browsers read files and servers alike). Chapter 1 explains every line; for now, celebrate — day zero complete.

The 3 technologies in one picture

Table 1 — HTML vs CSS vs JavaScript (the 10-second version)
TechnologyJobAnalogy
HTMLSTRUCTURE (headings, text, images, buttons)The skeleton and walls of a house
CSSDESIGN (colors, sizes, layout, animation)Paint, furniture and decoration
JavaScriptBEHAVIOR (clicks, logins, live data)Electricity and plumbing that respond

Change one word in your file, save, and refresh the browser — you just edited structure (HTML). Chapters 11+ teach design (CSS); chapters 23+ teach behavior (JavaScript). The whole book is this page, grown up.

Quick check — What does HTML do?
  1. Colors and layout
  2. Page structure and content
  3. Click behavior
  4. Nothing
Answer: B  ·  HTML = structure (skeleton); CSS = design (paint); JavaScript = behavior (electricity).

How to Use This Book

Read this first

This book teaches you full-stack web development — everything needed to build complete websites and web applications, from the page you see in the browser to the server and database behind it. It starts from absolute zero and ends at a professional level.

The promise of this book

If you read this book from the first chapter to the last, type every example with your own hands, and solve every exercise before looking at the solution — this book alone is enough. You will be able to build, publish and explain real full-stack projects.

How each chapter works

Every chapter follows the same rhythm so your brain always knows what is coming:

  1. Simple explanation first. Each idea starts with everyday words and a real-life analogy. No jargon before understanding.
  2. Exact technical detail second. After you "get it", you learn the precise professional version — the one used in documentation and job interviews.
  3. Complete runnable example. Not fragments. Every example is a full file you can save and run.
  4. Quick checks and exercises. Short questions inside the chapter, plus exercises with full solutions at the end of the chapter.
  5. Key takeaway boxes. Grey-gold boxes summarize what you must never forget.
Pro tip — How to get 10x more from this book

Type the code — do not copy-paste. Your fingers teach your brain. When an example works, break it on purpose: change one thing, predict what happens, then run it. That is how developers really learn.

Almost nothing. You need a computer with a web browser (Chrome or Edge is best) and a way to write text files. That is it. Web Foundations — How the Internet Really Works

Before writing a single tag, understand the machine you are building for: networks, browsers and servers.
A developer who understands the platform debugs in minutes what others debug in days.
Chapter 1

What Happens When You Open a Website

Beginner~ 90 min
The full journey of a web page — from your finger pressing Enter to pixels on the screen — explained with zero assumed knowledge.
In this chapter
  • The client-server story
  • DNS, IP and ports in plain words
  • TCP, TLS and HTTP requests
  • Front-end vs back-end vs full-stack
  • Your first tour of browser DevTools
Angela §1–§3Elzero fundamentalsMDN Web basics

The restaurant analogy (read this first)

Think of it like this — The Internet is a restaurant

You (the client) sit at a table and read the menu. The waiter (the browser) takes your order to the kitchen (the server). The kitchen cooks (runs code, reads the database) and the waiter brings your dish (the web page). You never enter the kitchen — you only talk to the waiter. The entire web works exactly like this: clients ask, servers answer.

Computers that ask for pages are called clients (your phone, your laptop). Computers that answer with pages are called servers — powerful machines in datacenters that stay on day and night waiting for requests.

Addresses of the web: DNS, IP and ports

Every server has a numeric address called an IP address, like 142.250.190.46. Humans hate numbers, so we invented names like google.com. Translating names into numbers is the job of the DNS (Domain Name System) — the phonebook of the Internet.

1. BROWSER ......... "What is the IP of google.com?" ----\ 2. DNS SERVER ...... "It is 142.250.190.46" <-------------/ 3. BROWSER ......... opens a connection to 142.250.190.46 4. SERVER .......... receives the request, prepares the page 5. BROWSER ......... receives files (HTML+CSS+JS) and draws the page
Figure 2 — What happens when you type google.com and press Enter

A port is like an apartment number inside one building (one IP). Web servers normally listen on port 443 (secure) or 80 (old, insecure). A full address is therefore IP + port, for example 142.250.190.46:443.

Table 6 — Words you must know from day one
WordSimple meaningExample
ClientThe device asking for pagesYour browser
ServerThe machine answering with pagesGoogle's computers
IP addressNumeric address of a machine142.250.190.46
DomainHuman name for an IPgoogle.com
DNSSystem translating domains to IPsPhonebook of the web
PortWhich service inside the machine443 = secure web
URLFull address of one pagehttps://site.com/news
Quick check — DNS translates…
  1. IP to domain
  2. Domain to IP
  3. HTML to CSS
  4. JS to Python
Answer: B  ·  DNS resolves human names like google.com into numeric IP addresses.

The three handshakes: TCP, TLS, HTTP

Three protocols (agreed languages) cooperate on every page load:

  1. TCP opens a reliable connection — like dialing a phone number and waiting for "hello?". Your browser and the server agree they can hear each other.
  2. TLS (the S in HTTPS) encrypts everything — like switching to a secret language nobody eavesdropping can understand. It also proves the server is really who it claims to be (certificates).
  3. HTTP is the actual conversation: the browser sends a request ("give me /news") and the server returns a response ("here it is, status 200" + the files).
Table 7 — HTTP versions in 30 seconds
VersionIdeaStatus
HTTP/1.1One request at a time per connection; simple textStill works everywhere
HTTP/2Many requests over one connection; fasterStandard today
HTTP/3Same idea over a faster transport (QUIC); best on mobileModern standard
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Type URL → DNS finds IP → TCP connects → TLS encrypts → HTTP asks and receives → browser draws. Memorize this chain; half of all web debugging is finding which link broke.

Front-end vs back-end vs full-stack

Table 8 — The three jobs of web development
JobRuns whereBuilt withThis book
Front-endIn the user's browserHTML, CSS, JavaScriptParts 2–4, 9
Back-endOn the serverNode.js, Express, databasesParts 6–8
Full-stackBothEverything aboveThe whole book
  • Front-end is everything the user sees and touches: layout, colors, buttons, animations.
  • Back-end is everything hidden: saving accounts, checking passwords, storing orders.
  • Full-stack means you can build both sides and connect them — the goal of this book.

The browser is not magic: how a page is drawn

When files arrive, the browser's engine performs the Critical Rendering Path:

HTML bytes ---> DOM tree (structure) ----\ +---> Render tree ---> Layout ---> Paint ---> Screen CSS bytes ----> CSSOM tree (styles) -----/ JavaScript .......................... can modify both trees (interactivity)
Figure 3 — The Critical Rendering Path (simplified)
  1. DOM tree — the browser turns HTML text into a tree of objects JavaScript can touch.
  2. CSSOM tree — it turns CSS into a tree of style rules.
  3. Render tree — structure + styles combined (invisible things like display: none are dropped).
  4. Layout — the browser measures every box: x, y, width, height.
  5. Paint — pixels are colored: text, backgrounds, borders, shadows.
Pro tip — Why this matters already

Slow websites usually break at Layout or Paint. Later you will learn the golden performance rule: animate transform and opacity only — they skip Layout and Paint and run on the GPU at 60 frames per second.

Your first look at DevTools (2 minutes)

DevTools is the X-ray machine built into your browser. Press F12 (or Ctrl+Shift+I) on any page right now.

Table 9 — The 4 DevTools panels you need first
PanelWhat it showsFirst trick to try
ElementsThe live HTML + CSS of the pageClick the arrow icon, hover page parts, change text live
ConsoleJavaScript errors and your own test codeType 2 + 2 and press Enter
NetworkEvery file the page downloadedReload and watch requests appear
ApplicationStored data: cookies, localStorageSee what sites remember about you
Try it yourself — Open DevTools now

Visit any website, press F12, find the Elements panel, double-click some headline text and rewrite it. Congratulations — you just "hacked" a page (only on your screen; reload restores it). Developers do this daily to experiment.

Interview question — What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?

Expected answer: "DNS resolves the domain to an IP, the browser opens a TCP connection, performs a TLS handshake for HTTPS, sends an HTTP request, receives the response, then parses HTML/CSS, builds DOM and CSSOM, and renders the page through layout and paint." Saying this chain calmly already puts you ahead of most juniors.

Exercise 1 — Explain it to a 10-year-old

Without looking back, explain DNS to a child in two sentences, then explain client vs server in two sentences.

Solution

DNS is like the contacts app on a phone: you tap a name (google.com) and it finds the real number (the IP address) to call. A client is the person ordering food; a server is the kitchen cooking it — the client asks, the server answers.

Exercise 2 — Spot the tier

For each of these, say front-end or back-end: (a) a dropdown menu animation, (b) checking a login password, (c) page colors and fonts, (d) saving a new user in the database.

Solution

(a) front-end (b) back-end (c) front-end (d) back-end. Rule of thumb: visible and interactive = front-end; hidden data and decisions = back-end.

The files of a website

Table 11 — The file types you will meet constantly
FileContainsRuns where

Warning — Never upload .env or passwords to GitHub

The .env file holds secrets (database passwords, API keys). Real companies have been hacked because a developer pushed .env to a public repository. You will learn the safe way in the Git and Security chapters.

Folders that make sense

A clean front-end project looks like this from week one:

my-website/ |-- index.html (home page) |-- about.html (second page) |-- css/ | |-- main.css (your styles) | +-- reset.css (optional: normalizes browser defaults) |-- js/ | +-- app.js (your JavaScript) +-- images/ |-- logo.svg +-- hero.webp
Figure 4 — A professional starter structure
Pro tip — Naming rules professionals follow

Lowercase only, no spaces (use -), English names, and extensions that match content (.html, .css, .js). My Photo.JPG breaks on real servers — my-photo.jpg never does.

Absolute vs relative paths (with zero confusion)

Imagine you are in the my-website folder above, editing index.html:

CODE  ·  Linking files relatively
<!-- Same folder: just the name -->
<a href="about.html">About us</a>
<!-- Inside a subfolder: folder/name -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/main.css">
<!-- One folder up: ../ means "go up" -->
<img src="../shared/logo.svg" alt="Logo">
<!-- Absolute web path: starts at site root -->
<a href="/products/shoes">Shoes</a>
Table 12 — Path cheat-sheet
WrittenMeaning
about.htmlFile next to this one
css/main.cssGo into css, take main.css
../logo.svgGo one folder up, take logo.svg
/img/x.pngFrom the website root, take img/x.png
https://...Full address on another site (external)
Warning — Case sensitivity: the silent killer

On Windows Logo.SVG and logo.svg are the same file. On real web servers (Linux) they are different files. If your image works on your PC but not online, wrong uppercase/lowercase is suspect #1. Always use lowercase.

Quick check — ../img/a.png from /site/pages/about.html points to…
  1. /site/pages/img/a.png
  2. /site/img/a.png
  3. /img/a.png
  4. Nowhere
Answer: B  ·  .. climbs from pages/ to site/, then enters img/.
Exercise 3 — Fix the broken site

A beginner wrote <img src="Images\Photo.JPG"> and it fails online but works on his PC. List every problem and the fix.

Solution

Three problems: (1) backslash \ — web paths always use forward slashes /; (2) uppercase folder and extension — servers are case-sensitive; (3) vague name. Fix: rename to images/photo.jpg and write <img src="images/photo.jpg" alt="...">.

Chapter 3

HTTP — The Conversation Between Browser and Server

Beginner~ 75 min
Requests, responses, methods and status codes: the shared language of the entire web, front and back.
In this chapter
  • Requests and responses
  • GET vs POST vs PUT/PATCH/DELETE
  • Status codes you must memorize
  • Headers in plain words
  • JSON, the data language
Angela §APIMDN HTTPTutorialspoint HTTP

Requests and responses

Every interaction is two halves: the browser sends a request, the server returns a response.

BROWSER SERVER | -- GET /products (request) ----------> | | <--------- 200 OK + JSON (response) -- | | -- POST /orders {shoes} (request) ---> | | <--------- 201 Created (response) ---- |
Figure 5 — An HTTP conversation

A request has: a method (what to do), a path (to what), headers (extra info) and sometimes a body (data). A response has: a status code (what happened), headers, and usually a body.

The five methods (verbs)

Table 13 — HTTP methods
MethodJobExampleSafe to repeat?
GETRead dataLoad productsYes (never changes data)
POSTCreate dataSubmit registrationNo (creates again!)
PUTReplace whole itemReplace product #5Yes
PATCHUpdate part of itemChange only the priceYes
DELETERemove itemDelete order #9Yes
Think of it like this — HTTP methods are restaurant verbs

GET = "show me the menu" (nothing changes). POST = "place a new order". PUT = "take my order back, here is a completely new one". PATCH = "same order, but no onions". DELETE = "cancel my order".

Status codes you must memorize

Table 14 — The 10 codes that cover 99% of real work
CodeNameMeaningWho caused it
200OKSuccess, here is your data—
201CreatedNew item saved—
204No ContentSuccess, nothing to return—
301MovedPage permanently moved (redirect)Server config
304Not ModifiedUse your cached copy—
400Bad RequestYour data is invalidClient
401UnauthorizedLog in firstClient
403ForbiddenLogged in, but not allowedClient
404Not FoundNo such page/itemClient
429Too Many RequestsSlow down (rate limit)Client
500Server ErrorBug in server codeServer
Pro tip — Read codes like a pro

2xx = success, 3xx = redirect/cache, 4xx = you (client) made a mistake, 5xx = the server made a mistake. When debugging, this single digit tells you which side to fix.

Headers in plain words

Headers are small labeled notes attached to requests and responses:

CODE  ·  Real headers, translated
Content-Type: application/json ...... "the body is JSON data"
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbG... ..... "this user is logged in, token attached"
Cache-Control: max-age=3600 ......... "you may reuse this for 1 hour"
Location: /login .................... "go here instead" (with 3xx)

You do not memorize headers now — just recognize the pattern Name: value.

JSON, the data language of the web

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is how front-end and back-end exchange data: text shaped like JavaScript objects.

CODE  ·  A product in JSON
{
  "id": 5,
  "name": "Running shoes",
  "price": 1299,
  "inStock": true,
  "sizes": [40, 41, 42, 43]
}
Table 15 — JSON rules (only 6 matter)
RuleExample
Keys always in double quotes"name" not 'name'
Strings in double quotes"Running shoes"
Numbers plain1299 (no quotes)
Booleans lowercasetrue / false
null for empty" discount ": null
No trailing commas[1, 2] not [1, 2,]
Quick check — A form submits but the server says 400. Who is wrong?
  1. The server crashed
  2. The client sent invalid data
  3. The Internet is down
  4. DNS failed
Answer: B  ·  4xx always means the request (client side) was wrong — here, validation failed.
Exercise 4 — Debug the status

For each case name the best status: (a) login with wrong password, (b) new article saved, (c) admin page visited by a normal user, (d) server code crashes.

Solution

(a) 401 Unauthorized (b) 201 Created (c) 403 Forbidden (d) 500 Internal Server Error. Note (a) vs (c): unknown/at-login problems are 401, known-user-but-not-allowed is 403.

Part

HTML — The Skeleton of Every Page

Structure first: tags, text, links, images, tables and forms.
Learn HTML deeply once, and every framework becomes easy.
Chapter 4

Your First HTML — Tags, Elements and the Page Skeleton

Beginner~ 90 min
What a tag really is, how elements nest, and the only page template you will ever need.
In this chapter
  • Tags vs elements vs attributes
  • The non-negotiable page skeleton
  • Headings and paragraphs done right
  • Comments and void elements
  • Your first complete page
Elzero HTML #1–#14Gamal HTML #1–#10Angela §HTML

Tags, elements, attributes — finally clear

Table 16 — The three words beginners mix up
WordWhat it isExample
TagThe angle-bracket marker<p> and </p>
ElementOpening tag + content + closing tag<p>Hello</p>
AttributeExtra info inside the opening taglang="en" in <html lang="en">
CODE  ·  The anatomy of an element
<p class="intro" id="first">Hello, web!</p>
|  |               |       |          |
|  attribute       attribute content  |
opening tag                         closing tag
Think of it like this — Tags are labeled boxes

An element is a labeled box: the opening tag writes the label (<p> = "this is a paragraph"), the content goes inside, the closing tag (</p>) seals the box. Attributes are sticky notes on the box ("class: intro").

Rules of nesting (3 rules, zero exceptions)

  1. Close in reverse order (last opened = first closed).
  2. Never overlap tags.
  3. Some elements can never contain anything — they are void elements.
CODE  ·  Nesting right vs wrong
<!-- RIGHT: perfect Russian dolls -->
<article><h2>Title</h2><p>Text with <strong>bold</strong> word.</p></article>

<!-- WRONG: overlapping (browsers guess, differently!) -->
<p>Text with <strong>bold</p></strong>

<!-- VOID elements: no closing tag, nothing inside -->
<img src="cat.webp" alt="A cat">
<br>
<hr>
<input type="text">
Warning — The #1 beginner bug

Forgetting that <img>, <br>, <hr>, <input>, <meta> and <link> are void: writing </img> or putting text inside them. Validate mentally: "can this hold content?" A picture cannot hold a paragraph — so no closing tag.

The only skeleton you need (memorize it)

CODE  ·  The professional HTML5 template
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <meta name="description" content="My first professional web page.">
  <title>My First Page</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/main.css">
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello, web!</h1>
  <p>This page follows every professional rule from day one.</p>
  <script src="js/app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
Table 17 — Skeleton lines, translated
LineWhy it exists
<!DOCTYPE html>Tells the browser "this is modern HTML5"
<html lang="en">Root element + language for screen readers and Google
<meta charset="UTF-8">Correct display of all languages and emojis
viewport metaMakes mobile show the real responsive layout (never skip!)
description metaThe text Google shows under your link
<title>Browser tab text + bookmark name
CSS in <head>Styles load before content (no unstyled flash)
<script> at body endPage shows first, code runs after
Quick check — Where does the page description for Google live?
  1. In <title>
  2. In meta description
  3. In <h1>
  4. In the URL
Answer: B  ·  <meta name="description"> feeds search-result snippets; <title> feeds the tab/link title.

Headings and paragraphs done right

CODE  ·  One h1, logical order, real paragraphs
<h1>Complete Guide to Coffee</h1>
<p>Coffee is a brewed drink prepared from roasted beans.</p>
<h2>History</h2>
<p>Centuries ago in Ethiopia…</p>
<h2>Brewing methods</h2>
<h3>Espresso</h3>
<p>Hot water forced through fine grounds…</p>
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Exactly one <h1> per page (the page topic), headings in order (h1 → h2 → h3, never h1 → h4), and paragraphs for text — never a heading chosen "because it looks big" (size is CSS's job).

Try it yourself — Your first page (10 minutes)

Create index.html with the skeleton above, change the title and text to describe yourself, open it in the browser by double-clicking. Then press F12 and find your <h1> in the Elements panel. You are now officially a web developer.

Exercise 5 — Fix this skeleton

This page shows ???? for Arabic text and looks tiny on phones. Two lines are missing. Which?

Solution

<meta charset="UTF-8"> (fixes ???? encoding) and <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> (fixes mobile zoom). These two lines belong in every page you ever write.

Chapter 5

Text, Links and Lists

Beginner~ 75 min
The elements that carry 90% of web content: formatting text, linking pages, and building menus.
In this chapter
  • Text formatting that means something
  • Links: internal, external, email, phone, downloads
  • Images vs buttons vs links

Elzero HTML #15–#28Gamal HTML #11–#20W3Schools HTML

Text formatting that MEANS something

HTML tags describe meaning, not looks. Screen readers and Google read the meaning.

Table 18 — Text elements by meaning
ElementMeaningUse when
<strong>ImportantWarnings, key terms (reads with emphasis)
<em>Stressed emphasis"You must save first"
<mark>HighlightedSearch results
<small>Fine printCopyrights, disclaimers
<del> / <ins>Deleted / insertedPrice changes, document edits
<code>Code fragmentlet x = 1
<time datetime="2026-09-07">Machine-readable dateEvents, articles
<br>Line breakPoems, addresses (rare!)
<hr>Topic changeBetween article sections
CODE  ·  Meaningful text in action
<p>Sale ends <time datetime="2026-09-30">September 30</time>:
<del>$99</del> <ins>$59</ins>. <strong>Tickets are limited</strong>,
so <em>please</em> book early. Use code <code>SAVE40</code>.</p>
Warning — `<b>` and `<i>` are last-century style

<strong>/<em> carry meaning; <b>/<i> are pure styling. In new code, default to <strong> and <em> — and do all visual styling in CSS anyway.

Links: the soul of the web

CODE  ·  Every link type you need
<!-- Internal page -->
<a href="about.html">About us</a>
<!-- Section inside this page -->
<a href="#pricing">See pricing</a>
<!-- External site: ALWAYS add rel for security -->
<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org" target="_blank" rel="noopener">MDN Docs</a>
<!-- Email and phone -->
<a href="mailto:[email protected]">Email us</a>
<a href="tel:+201141225852">Call us</a>
<!-- Download a file -->
<a href="files/menu.pdf" download>Download menu (PDF)</a>
Table 19 — Link rules professionals never break
RuleWhy
External + target="_blank" ⇒ add rel="noopener"Without it the new page can hijack yours (tabnabbing attack)
Link text describes the target"Read the pricing guide" beats "click here" for Google and blind users
href="#id" jumps to id="..."Powers tables of contents and "back to top"
download for filesTells the browser to save, not open

Lists: unordered, ordered, description

CODE  ·  All three list types
<!-- Bullets: order does not matter -->
<ul>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Bread</li>
</ul>
<!-- Numbers: order matters -->
<ol>
  <li>Boil water</li>
  <li>Add coffee</li>
  <li>Serve hot</li>
</ol>
<!-- Terms + definitions -->
<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt><dd>Structure of the page.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt><dd>Design of the page.</dd>
</dl>
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Navigation menus are <ul> lists of <a> links. Breadcrumbs, footers, dropdowns — all lists. If items look like "a set of similar things", reach for a list first.

Building a real navigation menu

CODE  ·  A professional navbar (structure only; CSS comes later)
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
  <ul>
    <li><a href="index.html" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="products.html">Products</a></li>
    <li><a href="about.html">About</a></li>
    <li><a href="contact.html">Contact</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

aria-label and aria-current are free accessibility wins: screen readers announce "Main navigation" and "current page: Home". You will master ARIA in Chapter 8.

Quick check — Which link is dangerous?
  1. <a href="/x">
  2. <a target="_blank" href="https://evil.com"> without rel
  3. <a href="#top">
  4. <a href="tel:+20">
Answer: B  ·  target="_blank" without rel="noopener" lets the new page control your tab. Always pair them.
Exercise 6 — Build a mini documentation page

Create a page with: an <h1>, a table of contents linking to 3 sections (# part1…), each section with <h2 id="...">, one external link (safe), and a "Back to top" link.

Solution

Structure: <a href="#part1">… items at top; <h2 id="part1"> etc. below; external link with target="_blank" rel="noopener"; <a href="#top"> with <body id="top"> (or an element id="top" at the start). Test every link by clicking.

Chapter 6

Images, Media and Tables

Beginner~ 90 min
Showing pictures, video and audio correctly — plus tables that are accessible, not just grids.
In this chapter
  • img done professionally (alt, sizes, lazy)
  • Modern formats: WebP, AVIF, SVG
  • figure + figcaption
  • Audio and video
  • Tables: thead, tbody, th scope, captions
Elzero HTML #29–#45Gamal HTML #21–#32Angela §HTML

Images done professionally

CODE  ·  The complete professional image
<img src="images/team.webp"
     alt="Our four-person team smiling in the Cairo office"
     width="800" height="450"
     loading="lazy">
Table 20 — Every image attribute, explained
AttributeJobRule
srcFile pathUse images/name.webp, lowercase, no spaces
altText replacement of the imageInformative images: describe. Decorative: alt="" (announces nothing)
width + heightReserve space before loadingPrevents layout jump (Core Web Vital: CLS)
loading="lazy"Load only when scrolled nearAll below-the-fold images; NEVER on the top hero image
Think of it like this — alt text is a phone call

Read your alt to a friend on the phone: can they picture the image? "IMG_2024" fails. "A barista pouring latte art shaped like a leaf" wins. If the image adds nothing (a decorative line), alt="" tells screen readers to skip it silently.

Modern formats (stop shipping heavy JPGs)

Table 21 — Which format when
FormatBest forWhy
SVGLogos, icons, diagramsVector = infinitely sharp, tiny size, styleable with CSS
WebPPhotos and general images~30% smaller than JPG, supported everywhere modern
AVIFLarge hero photos~50% smaller than JPG; add JPG/WebP fallback
JPGFallback photosUniversal compatibility
PNGScreenshots needing transparencyBigger; use only when needed
CODE  ·  Responsive art direction with picture
<picture>
  <source media="(min-width: 1024px)" srcset="images/hero-big.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source media="(min-width: 640px)" srcset="images/hero-mid.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="images/hero-small.jpg" alt="Cairo skyline at sunset"
       width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high">
</picture>

The browser picks the first <source> it supports; the <img> is the guaranteed fallback. fetchpriority="high" on the hero tells the browser "load this first".

Figures, audio and video

CODE  ·  Media elements complete
<figure>
  <img src="images/chart.svg" alt="Sales doubled from 2023 to 2026" width="600" height="300">
  <figcaption>Figure 1 — Company sales 2023–2026.</figcaption>
</figure>

<video controls width="640" preload="metadata" poster="images/talk-cover.webp">
  <source src="media/talk.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="media/talk.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Sorry, your browser cannot play this video.
</video>

<audio controls preload="none">
  <source src="media/episode.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
</audio>
Pro tip — Media performance rules

preload="none"/"metadata" for below-fold media, always controls unless you build custom controls with JavaScript, always a poster for video, and prefer WebM/MP3 with fallbacks.

Tables: data, not layout

Tables are for tabular data (prices, schedules, specs) — never for page layout (that was a 1999 hack; CSS Grid replaced it).

CODE  ·  An accessible professional table
<table>
  <caption>Course prices — 2026</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Course</th><th scope="col">Hours</th><th scope="col">Price</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><th scope="row">HTML Basics</th><td>10</td><td>$29</td></tr>
    <tr><th scope="row">CSS Mastery</th><td>25</td><td>$49</td></tr>
  </tbody>
  <tfoot>
    <tr><th scope="row">Bundle</th><td>35</td><td>$59</td></tr>
  </tfoot>
</table>
Table 22 — Table elements
ElementJob
<caption>Table title (announced first by screen readers)
<thead> / <tbody> / <tfoot>Header / body / footer groups (also help printing + styling)
<th scope="col">Column header ("this labels the column below")
<th scope="row">Row header ("this labels the row beside")
<td>Normal data cell
colspan / rowspanMerge cells across columns / rows
Quick check — Why width+height on img?
  1. Bigger images
  2. Reserves space, prevents layout shift
  3. Required by HTML
  4. Faster download
Answer: B  ·  Reserved aspect-ratio space stops content jumping when images load (fixes CLS).
Exercise 7 — Accessible schedule table

Build a weekly class schedule: caption, thead with Day/Topic/Time, 3 tbody rows with scope="row" day names, tfoot with total hours. Then view it with images off — it must still make full sense.

Solution

Follow the course-price template: <caption>Weekly schedule</caption>, <th scope="col"> for Day/Topic/Time, each row starting <th scope="row">Saturday</th>, tfoot summing hours. Screen-reader test: each data cell is announced with its headers.

Chapter 7

Forms — Collecting Data Like a Pro

Beginner+~ 120 min
Labels, inputs, validation and accessible forms: the bridge between your page and the server.
In this chapter
  • form, label, input trio
  • Every input type with examples

Elzero HTML #46–#62Gamal HTML #33–#45Angela §Forms

The golden trio: form + label + input

CODE  ·  The smallest correct form
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required autocomplete="email">
  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>
Table 23 — The trio, translated
PieceJobDeadly sin
<form action method>Where data goes + how (get = in URL, post = in body)Forgetting action (submits to same page randomly)
<label for="id">Clickable name of the fieldPlaceholder instead of label (vanishes, inaccessible)
<input name>The field; name becomes the data key sent to the serverMissing name = field silently never sent
<button type="submit">Sends the form<button> without type inside forms defaults to submit (surprise!)
Think of it like this — Labels are name tags at a party

for="email" on the label must exactly match id="email" on the input — like calling someone by their exact name tag. Clicking the label then focuses the input (try it!). Screen readers also announce "Email address, edit text" only when this link exists.

Every input type (with when to use it)

CODE  ·  The input zoo — each with its keyboard and validation
<label>Text <input type="text" name="city" maxlength="40" placeholder="Cairo"></label>
<label>Email <input type="email" name="email" required></label>
<label>Password <input type="password" name="pw" minlength="8" required autocomplete="new-password"></label>
<label>Age <input type="number" name="age" min="13" max="120"></label>
<label>Birthday <input type="date" name="dob"></label>
<label>Meeting <input type="datetime-local" name="meet"></label>
<label>Favorite color <input type="color" name="color" value="#2563eb"></label>
<label>Volume <input type="range" name="vol" min="0" max="100" value="70"></label>
<label>Avatar <input type="file" name="avatar" accept="image/*"></label>
<label>Phone <input type="tel" name="phone" pattern="[0-9+ ]{8,15}"></label>
<label>Website <input type="url" name="site" placeholder="https://…"></label>
<input type="hidden" name="source" value="landing-page">
Table 24 — Choosing types like a senior
NeedTypeBonus you get free
EmailemailMobile shows @ keyboard + format check
Numbersnumber + min/maxSpinners + range validation
Secret textpasswordHidden dots + manager support
Pick one of fewradio (same name)Arrow-key navigation
Pick manycheckboxIndependent on/off values
Long text<textarea rows>Resizable multiline
Big option list<select> + <option>Native dropdown, searchable on mobile

Built-in validation (free, before JavaScript)

CODE  ·  Validation without a single line of JS
<form action="/register" method="post">
  <label for="user">Username (3–12 letters)</label>
  <input id="user" name="user" required minlength="3" maxlength="12" pattern="[A-Za-z]+"
         title="Letters only, 3 to 12 characters">
  <label for="pw2">Password (8+ chars, 1 digit)</label>
  <input id="pw2" type="password" name="pw" required
         pattern="(?=.*\d).{8,}" title="At least 8 characters including one digit">
  <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>
Table 25 — Validation attributes
AttributeEffect
requiredBlocks submit when empty
minlength / maxlengthText length limits
min / max / stepNumber/date limits
pattern (regex)Custom format rule + title explains it
type=email/url/numberFormat validation included
Warning — Never trust the browser alone

Built-in validation is UX sugar — attackers bypass it in seconds. The server MUST validate everything again (you will build that in Chapters 39–40). Rule: validate in browser for speed, on server for safety.

Select, radio, checkbox, fieldset

CODE  ·  Grouped choices, accessibly
<fieldset>
  <legend>Delivery options</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="ship" value="fast" checked> Fast (2 days)</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="ship" value="slow"> Slow (7 days, free)</label>
</fieldset>
<label for="pay">Payment</label>
<select id="pay" name="pay" required>
  <option value="">— Choose —</option>
  <option value="card">Credit card</option>
  <option value="cash">Cash on delivery</option>
</select>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="news" checked> Email me offers</label>
<label for="notes">Notes</label>
<textarea id="notes" name="notes" rows="4" maxlength="500"></textarea>

<fieldset> + <legend> groups related controls with a real announced title — the accessible way to say "these belong together".

Quick check — Radio buttons in one group must share…
  1. id
  2. name
  3. value
  4. type
Answer: B  ·  Same name = one group (browser enforces single choice); each keeps its own value and unique id.
Exercise 8 — Complete registration form

Build: username (required, 3–12 letters), email (required), password (required, 8+ with digit), gender (radio: she/he, required), country (select with 4 options), bio (textarea, max 200), terms checkbox (required). Every control labeled, grouped with fieldset/legend.

Solution

Follow the patterns above: labels with matching for/id, shared name="gender" radios, first <option value=""> placeholder, required on terms checkbox. Submit empty to watch the browser block you with messages — that is built-in validation working.

Chapter 8

Semantic HTML, Accessibility and SEO

Beginner+~ 90 min
Write pages that Google loves and everyone can use — including people who cannot see the screen.
In this chapter
  • div-soup vs semantic landmarks
  • header/nav/main/article/section/aside/footer
  • ARIA when HTML is not enough
  • Alt, labels, contrast, keyboard
  • SEO basics that actually matter
Elzero HTML #63–#75Gamal HTML #46–#55MDN ARIA

Div-soup vs landmarks

CODE  ·  Before — meaningless div soup
<div id="header"><div class="nav">…</div></div>
<div id="main"><div class="post">…</div></div>
<div id="footer">…</div>

<!-- After — a blind user can "jump to main content" -->
<header><nav aria-label="Main">…</nav></header>
<main>
  <article><h1>…</h1><p>…</p></article>
  <aside><h2>Related</h2>…</aside>
</main>
<footer>…</footer>
Table 26 — Landmark elements
ElementMeaningRule
<header>Intro of page or sectionLogo/nav inside; not <head> (head = metadata!)
<nav>Major navigation blockOnly main navs, not every link group
<main>The page's unique core contentExactly ONE per page
<article>Self-contained piece (post, card, comment)Must make sense alone / shareable
<section>Thematic group, usually with headingNo heading? Probably a <div>
<aside>Tangentially relatedSidebars, related links
<footer>Closing infoCopyright, contacts, sitemap links
<div>No meaning — styling/layout boxThe honest fallback
<span>No meaning — inline styling hookInside text only
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

<article> vs <section> vs <div>: could it be shared alone (a post)? → <article>. Is it a themed chunk with a heading (Pricing, Reviews)? → <section>. Just a box for styling? → <div>. This single test ends 90% of semantic debates.

ARIA: when HTML needs a microphone

Native elements come with free accessibility (buttons are clickable by keyboard, inputs announce labels). Only when building custom widgets do you add ARIA attributes:

CODE  ·  ARIA essentials
<!-- Custom widget: tell assistive tech what it is and its state -->
<div role="alert">Saved successfully.</div>
<button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="menu">Menu</button>
<nav id="menu" aria-label="Main navigation">…</nav>
<img src="deco.svg" alt="" aria-hidden="true">
Table 27 — ARIA survival kit
AttributeMeaning
role="alert/dialog/button""Treat this div as…" (last resort — prefer real elements!)
aria-label="Close"Invisible name for icon-only buttons
aria-current="page""This nav link is the current page"
aria-expanded / aria-controlsWidget open/closed state + what it controls
aria-hidden="true" + alt="""Skip this decoration entirely"
Warning — First rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA

A real <button> beats <div role="button"> (free keyboard, focus, clicks). A real <input type="checkbox"> beats a custom one. Reach for ARIA only when HTML truly has no element for the job.

The accessibility checklist (WCAG in 1 page)

Ship nothing without these
  • - Every img has correct alt (or alt="" for decoration)
  • - Every input has a matching <label for>
  • - Color contrast ≥ 4.5:1 for text (check with DevTools → CSS overview)
  • - Everything clickable works with keyboard alone (Tab + Enter)
  • - Focus is always visible (never outline: none without a replacement)
  • - Page has one <h1>, logical heading order, <html lang>
  • - aria-label on icon-only buttons; aria-current in nav
  • - Videos have captions; audio has transcripts

SEO basics that actually matter

CODE  ·  SEO head starter
<title>Fresh Coffee Beans in Cairo — Roastly</title>
<meta name="description" content="Order freshly roasted coffee beans in Cairo. Same-day delivery, 12 origins.">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://roastly.example/">
<meta property="og:title" content="Roastly — Fresh Coffee Beans">
<meta property="og:description" content="Same-day delivery in Cairo.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://roastly.example/images/og.jpg">
Table 28 — SEO that works in 2026
DoWhy
One clear <title> + honest description per pageThis is your Google listing
Semantic headings with real keywordsGoogle reads structure, not font sizes
Fast + mobile-friendly (viewport, WebP, lazy)Speed is a ranking factor
Descriptive alt + filenamesImage search traffic is free traffic
Open Graph tagsPretty previews when shared on social apps
lang, sitemap, HTTPSBasics Google expects from serious sites
Quick check — Best page title?
  1. Home
  2. Roastly
  3. Fresh Coffee Beans in Cairo — Roastly
  4. CLICK HERE!!!
Answer: C  ·  Specific + keyword + brand. "Home" tells Google nothing; keyword-stuffing hurts.
Exercise 9 — Accessibility audit

Take your Chapter 6 page: unplug the mouse and use only Tab/Enter — can you reach everything? Then run Lighthouse in DevTools (Audits tab) and fix every Accessibility item until the score is 95+.

Solution

Typical fixes: add missing alts, pair every label, raise grey-on-white contrast to 4.5:1, add :focus-visible styles, give the nav aria-label. Re-run Lighthouse to verify — green scores are the proof.

Chapter 9

Project — Personal Profile Page (HTML only)

Beginner+~ 120 min
Assemble everything from Part 2 into one complete, semantic, accessible page. No CSS yet — structure must shine alone.

Step 4 — Self-review checklist

Profile page review
  • - Exactly one <h1>; headings in order; landmarks header/nav/main/footer present
  • - All images have alt + width/height; below-fold ones loading="lazy"
  • - Form: labels match ids, names set, required where needed
  • - Keyboard-only navigation works; try unplugging the mouse
  • - No <div> where <section>/<article>/<nav> fits; no <br> for spacing
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

If your page makes full sense with CSS turned off (DevTools → Rendering → disable CSS), your HTML is excellent. Structure first, beauty second — always.

Chapter 10

HTML Datasheet — Every Important Tag in One Place

Reference~ 60 min
The quick-lookup chapter: find any tag in seconds, see what it does and copy a correct example.
In this chapter
  • Document tags
  • Text tags
  • Links & media
  • Lists & tables
  • Forms & semantic — all with examples
DatasheetW3Schools refMDN ref

Use this chapter during real work: each card shows the tag, what it is for, a correct example, and the one thing to remember.

!DOCTYPEDocument
Declaration (not a tag) that switches the browser to standards mode. Must be the very first line.
<!DOCTYPE html>
key: Without it browsers enter "quirks mode" and CSS behaves like 1999.
htmlDocument
Root element wrapping the whole page. Always set lang for screen readers and search engines.
<html lang="en">…</html>
key: lang="en" (or "ar" for Arabic) changes pronunciation of screen readers.
headDocument
Invisible metadata container: title, meta tags, CSS links. Nothing here is displayed.
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>Shop</title></head>
key: CSS links go here; page JS usually goes at the end of body.
meta charsetMetadata
Declares UTF-8 encoding so all languages and emojis display correctly.
<meta charset="UTF-8">
key: First tag inside head, always.
meta viewportMetadata
Tells mobile browsers to use the real device width — the foundation of responsive design.
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
key: Missing viewport = broken mobile layout. Never skip.
titleMetadata
Browser tab text, bookmark name and the clickable Google headline.
<title>Fresh Coffee in Cairo — Roastly</title>
key: Unique per page, under ~60 characters.
h1–h6Text
Headings level 1 (page topic) to 6 (deep sub-topic). Structure, not font size.
<h1>Guide</h1><h2>History</h2><h3>Early years</h3>
key: One h1 per page; never skip levels.
pText
A paragraph of text. Browsers add spacing automatically.
<p>Shipping is free over $50.</p>
key: Never use <br><br> to fake paragraphs.
aLinks
Hyperlink to pages, sections (#id), files, email (mailto:) or phone (tel:).
<a href="about.html">About</a>
<a href="https://x.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">X</a>
key: External + new tab ⇒ always rel="noopener".
strong / emText meaning
Important (strong) and stressed (em) text — announced with emphasis by screen readers.
<p><strong>Warning:</strong> save <em>before</em> closing.</p>
key: Meaning first; style with CSS.
ul / ol / liLists
Unordered (bullets), ordered (numbered) lists and their items. Menus are ul of links.
<ul><li>Milk</li><li>Bread</li></ul>
<ol><li>Boil</li><li>Brew</li></ol>
key: li must be a direct child of ul/ol.
imgMedia
Embeds an image. src = path, alt = replacement text, width/height reserve space.
<img src="cat.webp" alt="Sleeping cat" width="600" height="400" loading="lazy">
key: Informative ⇒ describe; decorative ⇒ alt="".
picture / sourceMedia
Art direction: serve different/better formats per screen, with img fallback.
<picture><source srcset="big.avif" type="image/avif"><img src="small.jpg" alt="…"></picture>
key: Browser takes the first source it supports.
figure / figcaptionMedia
Self-contained media with a caption (diagrams, photos, code screenshots).
<figure><img src="c.svg" alt="…"><figcaption>Fig 1 — Sales.</figcaption></figure>
key: Caption belongs to the figure, moves with it.
video / audioMedia
Native players. Multiple sources = format fallbacks; text inside = last-resort fallback.
<video controls width="640" poster="p.webp"><source src="v.webm" type="video/webm"></video>
key: Always controls unless you build custom JS controls.
table / thead / tbody / tfootTables
Table with header/body/footer groups. caption first; th for headers, td for data.
<table><caption>Prices</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Item</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>X</td></tr></tbody></table>
key: Tables are for data — never for layout.
formForms
Collects inputs and submits to action via method get (URL) or post (body).
<form action="/signup" method="post">…</form>
key: Every submittable control needs a name.
labelForms
Accessible name of a control. for must equal the control's id.
<label for="e">Email</label><input id="e" type="email" name="email">
key: Clicking the label focuses the input — test it.
inputForms
One-line field; type changes behavior: text email password number date file checkbox radio range color tel url.
<input type="email" name="email" required>
key: Missing name ⇒ value never sent to the server.
textarea / select / optionForms
Multiline text; dropdown list with options. First empty option = placeholder.
<textarea name="msg" rows="4"></textarea>
<select name="pay"><option value="">— Choose —</option><option value="card">Card</option></select>
key: select needs required + empty first option for "must choose".
buttonForms
Clickable button. Types: submit (send), reset (clear), button (JS only).
<button type="submit">Save</button><button type="button" id="more">Load more</button>
key: Inside forms, typeless button = submit (common bug).
header / nav / main / footerLandmarks
Page intro, navigation, unique content (one only), closing info.
<header><nav>…</nav></header><main>…</main><footer>…</footer>
key: Landmarks let screen-reader users jump around the page.
article / section / asideSemantic
Shareable piece (article), themed group with heading (section), tangential content (aside).
<article><h2>Post</h2></article><section><h2>Pricing</h2></section><aside>Related</aside>
key: No heading and no independent meaning ⇒ plain div.
div / spanGeneric
Meaningless block (div) and inline (span) containers for styling and JS hooks.
<div class="card"><span class="price">$9</span></div>
key: Honest fallback — but check semantic options first.
script / linkResources
link loads CSS in head; script loads JS (end of body, or head with defer).
<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/main.css">
<script src="js/app.js" defer></script>
key: defer = download now, run after HTML parsed. Best default.

CSS First Steps — Selectors and Ways to Style

How CSS talks to HTML: rules, selectors, and the three places styles can live.

Elzero CSS #1–#15Gamal CSS #1–#12Angela §CSS

A CSS rule in 10 seconds

CODE  ·  The anatomy of a rule
h1 {
  color: navy;
  font-size: 32px;
}
|   |      |
|   |      value
|   property
selector (who to style)

A selector picks elements; declarations (property: value;) describe the styling. Forget a semicolon or brace and the whole rule dies silently — CSS never shows errors, it just ignores mistakes.

Warning — CSS fails silently

A typo like colour: red or a missing } breaks styling with ZERO error messages. When "CSS doesn't work", suspect #1 is always a typo. DevTools → Elements → Styles shows crossed-out invalid lines.

The selectors you will use daily

Table 29 — Core selectors
SelectorPicksExample
pAll paragraphsp { … }
.cardAll elements with class="card"The workhorse — reuse everywhere
#menuThe single element with id="menu"Unique things only
*EverythingResets only (never for real styling)
h1, h2, pGroups (any listed)Shared rules in one place
.card p<p> inside .card (any depth)Descendant
.menu > liDirect children onlyTop-level items, not nested ones
input[type="email"]By attributeEmail fields specifically
a:hoverOn mouse hoverInteractive states
li:first-childFirst child of its parentFirst items, no classes needed
CODE  ·  Selectors in action
/* All cards share the box look */
.card { border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 16px; }
/* Only paragraphs INSIDE cards get this color */
.card p { color: #333; }
/* The one hero title */
#hero-title { font-size: 48px; }
/* Email fields glow on focus */
input[type="email"]:focus { outline: 2px solid navy; }
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Classes for styling (reusable), IDs for JS hooks and anchors (unique). If you styled with #id everywhere, you cannot reuse the style — seniors style with classes ~95% of the time.

Combining selectors (read right-to-left)

CODE  ·  Reading selectors like a senior
/* "Links inside list items inside .menu" */
.menu li a { text-decoration: none; }
/* "Direct li children of .menu" (excludes nested dropdown items) */
.menu > li { display: inline-block; }
/* "Paragraphs that come right after an h2" (intro paragraphs) */
h2 + p { font-size: 18px; }
/* "Any p after an h2 until the next heading" */
h2 ~ p { color: #444; }
Table 30 — Combinators
SymbolNameMeaning
(space)DescendantAnywhere inside
>ChildDirect child only
+Adjacent siblingThe very next sibling
~General siblingAny later sibling

Three places CSS can live (use only one!)

CODE  ·  The three ways — and the winner
<!-- 1. EXTERNAL (the professional way): one file styles the whole site -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/main.css">

<!-- 2. INTERNAL: <style> in head — only for single-page experiments -->
<style>h1 { color: navy; }</style>

<!-- 3. INLINE: style="" — emergencies and JS only, never for real styling -->
<h1 style="color: navy;">Hi</h1>
Table 31 — Where to put CSS
WayUse whenProblem
External .css fileAlways (real projects)None — cached, shared, clean
<style> in headQuick single-page testsCannot share across pages
style="" inlineJS dynamic styles, HTML emailsUnreusable, beats all specificity, unmaintainable
Quick check — Best selector for "all submit buttons site-wide"?
  1. #submit
  2. button.submit-btn class
  3. div > div > button
  4. *
Answer: B  ·  A class is reusable and readable; IDs can't repeat; long chains are brittle.
Exercise 10 — Selector gym

Given <nav class="menu"><ul><li><a>Home</a></li></ul></nav>: write selectors for (a) the nav, (b) all links in it, (c) links on hover turning gold.

Solution

(a) .menu (b) .menu a (c) .menu a:hover { color: gold; }. Note (b) uses a descendant selector — short, robust, reusable.

Chapter 12

The Cascade, Specificity and Inheritance

Beginner+~ 90 min
Why one rule wins over another: the scoring system browsers use on every element.
In this chapter
  • Cascade order (origin + position)
  • Specificity scoring 0-0-0
  • !important and why to avoid it
  • Inheritance: what passes to children
  • Debugging conflicts in DevTools
Elzero CSS #16–#25Gamal CSS #13–#20W3Schools CSS

The cascade: three rounds of battle

When rules collide, the browser decides in this order:

  1. Origin & importance: your styles beat browser defaults; !important beats everything normal.
  2. Specificity: the most specific selector wins (scored below).
  3. Position: if still tied, the LAST rule in the file wins.
CODE  ·  Position decides ties
p { color: red; }
p { color: navy; }   /* wins: same specificity, comes later */

Specificity scoring (count 0-0-0)

Selector ............ IDs | Classes/attrs/pseudo | Elements .... Score p ................... 0 | 0 | 1 .... 0-0-1 .card ............... 0 | 1 | 0 .... 0-1-0 .menu li a .......... 0 | 1 | 2 .... 0-1-2 #nav .item .......... 1 | 1 | 0 .... 1-1-0 (winner) style="" ............ beats everything (except !important)
Figure 7 — Specificity scoreboard: ID - CLASS - ELEMENT
CODE  ·  Specificity in action
/* 0-0-1 */
a { color: blue; }
/* 0-1-1 — wins over the rule above */
.menu a { color: white; }
/* 1-0-0 — wins over both */
#special-link { color: gold; }
Think of it like this — Specificity is a medal table

Countries rank by gold first, then silver, then bronze: 1 gold beats 100 silvers. Likewise 1 ID beats any number of classes, and 1 class beats any number of elements. Compare left column first — only move right on ties.

Warning — The !important trap

color: red !important bullies past everything — so the next developer adds a bigger !important, then another… Soon nothing can be overridden and the stylesheet is unfixable. Allowed only for: utility classes (.hidden) and overriding third-party code you cannot edit. If you use it weekly, your specificity structure is sick.

Inheritance: what children get for free

Some properties inherit (children copy the parent's value), others don't:

Table 32 — Inherits vs doesn't
Inherits (set once on body)Never inherits (set per element)
color, font-family, font-size, line-height, text-align, letter-spacingmargin, padding, border, background, width, display, position
CODE  ·  Set typography once, use everywhere
body {
  font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
  color: #222;
  line-height: 1.6;
}
/* Every p, li, td now inherits these — zero repetition */

Special values: inherit (force copy parent), initial (browser default), unset (inherit if inheritable else initial).

Debugging conflicts in DevTools

Try it yourself — See the battle live (3 minutes)

Open any page → F12 → Elements → select a heading → look at the Styles panel. Winning rules are on top; losing rules are crossed out with the winner's selector visible. This panel alone solves most "why is my CSS ignored?" mysteries.

Interview question — How do you handle CSS specificity wars?

Expected: "I keep specificity low and flat — mostly single classes — so order decides; I avoid IDs in CSS and never use !important except for utilities; I debug in DevTools Styles panel where losers are crossed out."

Quick check — .a .b (0-2-0) vs #x (1-0-0): who wins?
  1. .a .b (more selectors)
  2. #x (an ID beats any classes)
  3. Tie → later wins
  4. Neither
Answer: B  ·  IDs outrank everything in the classes column, no matter how many classes there are.
Exercise 11 — Score these

Rank weakest→strongest: h1, .title, #main .title, #main, body h1.title.

Solution

h1 (0-0-1) < body h1.title (0-1-2)… wait, compare properly: h1 = 0-0-1; body h1.title = 0-1-2; .title = 0-1-0; #main = 1-0-0; #main .title = 1-1-0. Order: h1 < .title < body h1.title < #main < #main .title. Remember: classes column beats elements column entirely.

The Box Model — Every Element Is a Box

Beginner+~ 100 min
Content, padding, border, margin — plus the box-sizing fix every professional applies on day one.
In this chapter

  • content-box vs border-box (the big fix)
  • Margin collapsing
  • Developer box inspector

Elzero CSS #26–#35Gamal CSS #21–#30Angela §CSS

The 4 layers

+-- MARGIN (transparent gap OUTSIDE, separates from neighbors) --+ | +-- BORDER (visible edge line) ---------------------------+ | | | +-- PADDING (space INSIDE, around content) ---------+ | | | | | +-- CONTENT (text/images: width x height) ---+ | | | | | | | Hello, I am the content. | | | | | | | +------------------------------------------+ | | | | | +------------------------------------------------+ | | | +------------------------------------------------------+ | +------------------------------------------------------------+
Figure 8 — Every element is 4 nested boxes
CODE  ·  The 4 layers in code
.card {
  width: 300px;               /* content width */
  padding: 20px;              /* inner breathing room */
  border: 2px solid navy;     /* visible edge */
  margin: 24px auto;          /* outside gap + horizontal centering */
}
Table 33 — Shorthand clock (1–4 values)
WrittenTopRightBottomLeft
margin: 10px10101010
margin: 10px 20px10201020
margin: 10px 20px 30px10203020
margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px10 ⬆20 ➡30 ⬇40 ⬅ (clockwise from top)

content-box vs border-box (the fix of the century)

The browser default (content-box) makes width count content only: padding and border are added ON TOP, so width: 300px + padding: 20px + border: 2px = 344px of real width. Layouts break mysteriously.

CODE  ·  The universal fix — first lines of every pro stylesheet
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
Table 34 — The difference that breaks layouts
Rulecontent-box (default)border-box (professional)
width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 2pxReal width = 344px (300+40+4)Real width = 300px exactly
Two 50% columns + paddingOverflow to next line (broken!)Fit perfectly
Mental model"Width plus extras""Width means width" (sane)
Think of it like this — Pizza box vs pizza

content-box: you order a 30cm pizza and get a 36cm box (pizza + walls + padding). border-box: you order a 30cm box and the pizza shrinks to fit inside. Professionals always think in boxes — so border-box everywhere.

Margin collapsing (the surprise)

Vertical margins of neighbors merge instead of adding: margin-bottom: 20px meeting margin-top: 30px = 30px gap, not 50px.

Table 35 — Collapsing rules
CaseResult
Two siblings (20px meets 30px)30px (bigger wins)
Parent + first child top marginsMerge through the parent (child "pulls" parent down!)
Empty element's own top/bottomCollapse into one
Horizontal margins (left/right)NEVER collapse — always add
Flex/Grid children (gap)NEVER collapse — use gap instead
CODE  ·  Fixes for collapsing headaches
/* Option 1: use padding on parent instead of margin on child */
.parent { padding-top: 30px; }  /* instead of child margin-top */
/* Option 2: modern layouts use gap (Ch 17-18), margins never meet */
/* Option 3: one-direction margins: only margin-bottom everywhere */

The box inspector + centering patterns

Try it yourself — Inspect the box (2 minutes)

F12 → Elements → select any element → look at the Computed/Box panel: a colored diagram shows exact content/padding/border/margin in pixels. Hover it to highlight each layer on the page. This is how pros measure "why is there a gap here?".

CODE  ·  Patterns you will reuse forever
/* Center a fixed-width block */
.container { width: 100%; max-width: 1100px; margin: 0 auto; }
/* One-direction spacing system */
.stack > * + * { margin-top: 16px; }  /* every child except first */
/* Reset killing browser default margins */
h1, h2, h3, p, ul { margin: 0 0 12px 0; }
Quick check — width:200px; padding:20px with border-box = ?
  1. 240px wide
  2. 200px wide, content 160px
  3. 200px content
  4. Error
Answer: B  ·  Border-box keeps total 200px; content shrinks to 200−40=160px.
Exercise 12 — Box math

.box { width: 400px; padding: 25px; border: 5px solid; margin: 10px; } — real rendered width in content-box vs border-box (excluding margin)?

Solution

content-box: 400 + 50 + 10 = 460px. border-box: 400px exactly (content becomes 340px). Margin (10px each side) sits outside both — never part of width.

In this chapter

Gamal CSS typographyElzero CSS unitsDeep-dive

DEEP-DIVE 1: font-size vs font-weight

Juniors constantly mix these two. They control completely different things:

Table 36 — font-size vs font-weight — the full truth
font-sizefont-weight
ControlsSpatial scale: how tall/wide letters areStroke thickness: how heavy/black the strokes are
AnalogyZoom level of the textThickness of the pen
Unitspx, rem, em, %, vw, clamp()Numbers 100–900 or normal/bold
Layout effectChanges element height, line boxes, wrapping(Almost) no layout change — same box, thicker ink
Example pairfont-size: 12px vs 48pxfont-weight: 400 vs 800
AccessibilityUse rem so users can scale textThin weights (100–300) can fail contrast on cheap screens
CODE  ·  Same sentence, four personalities
.tiny-bold   { font-size: 12px; font-weight: 800; }  /* small but shouts */
.huge-light  { font-size: 48px; font-weight: 200; }  /* big but whispers */
.body        { font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 400; }  /* normal reading */
.display     { font-size: 3rem; font-weight: 700; }  /* hero headline */
Table 37 — The 100–900 weight scale
ValueNameUsed for
100–200Thin / Extra LightHuge elegant headlines only
300LightLarge subtitles (careful with contrast)
400Normal / RegularALL body text default
500MediumSlightly emphasized UI text
600Semi BoldSub-headings
700BoldHeadings (<strong> default)
800–900Extra Bold / BlackDisplay headlines, badges, numbers
Warning — Faux bold: the blurry lie

If you request font-weight: 800 but loaded only weight 400, the browser fakes thickness by smearing pixels (faux bold) — ugly and blurry. Fix: load the real weights you use (Google Fonts → select 400;600;800), or use variable fonts.

Try it yourself — Feel the difference (1 minute)

In DevTools, select a headline and toggle font-weight 300→900 (box barely changes), then toggle font-size 12px→48px (layout explodes). Your eyes now permanently know the difference.

Units: px vs rem vs em vs % vs vw

Table 38 — Units decision table
UnitMeansUse forAvoid for
pxScreen pixels (fixed)Borders, shadows, tiny detailsBody font-size (blocks user scaling)
rem× root (<html>) font-sizeALL font sizes, spacing, widths—
em× parent's font-sizePadding that scales with its own text (buttons, badges)Nested font sizes (compounds confusingly!)
%× parent's same propertyFluid widths (width: 50%)Font sizes (same compounding trap as em)
vw/vh× viewport width/heightFull-screen heroes (min-height: 100vh)Body text (too extreme on huge/small screens)
chWidth of "0" glyphReadable line length (max-width: 65ch)—
CODE  ·  The professional unit system
html { font-size: 16px; }              /* 1rem = 16px baseline */
body { font-size: 1rem; }              /* 16px, user-scalable ✔ */
h1 { font-size: 2.5rem; }              /* 40px, scales with user setting ✔ */
.card { padding: 1.5rem; max-width: 65ch; }
.btn { font-size: 0.9rem; padding: 0.6em 1.2em; }  /* em: padding hugs text */
.hero { min-height: 90vh; }
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

rem for sizes, em for text-hugging padding, % for fluid widths, px for hairlines. And the accessibility law: a user who sets their browser to 24px default must get a fully working site — only rem-based typography guarantees that.

Quick check — Which respects browser font-size settings?
  1. px
  2. rem
  3. Both equally
  4. Neither
Answer: B  ·  rem multiplies the user's root size; px ignores it. That's why body text uses rem.

DEEP-DIVE 2: width vs max-width, height vs min-height

Table 39 — Fixed vs fluid — the responsive truth
RuleBehaviorVerdict
width: 600pxAlways 600px — overflows phones (375px!) with horizontal scrollAvoid for layout containers
width: 100%; max-width: 1100pxFills phones, stops growing on wide screensTHE container pattern — memorize it
height: 250pxRigid box — long text overflows and collides belowAnti-pattern for text containers
min-height: 250pxAt least 250px, grows with contentCorrect for heroes, cards, sections
aspect-ratio: 16/9Height auto-follows widthModern way for media boxes
CODE  ·  The two patterns behind 90% of professional layouts
/* Pattern 1: centered fluid container */
.container { width: 100%; max-width: 1100px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 0 16px; }
/* Pattern 2: elastic card that never overflows */
.card { min-height: 220px; }           /* grows if text grows ✔ */
.media { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }       /* video box keeps shape ✔ */
Think of it like this — Fixed vs elastic

width/height are glass boxes: exact size, contents spill if bigger. max-width/min-height are balloons with limits: they fit their space but never exceed (or shrink below) your rule. Responsive design = balloons everywhere, glass almost nowhere.

Warning — height + text = overflow bug

The #1 responsive bug in junior portfolios: a card with height: 200px whose Arabic/English text wraps to 3 lines on mobile and spills over the next card. Fix: min-height instead — always.

line-height: the unitless law

CODE  ·  Unitless (correct) vs px (dangerous)
body { line-height: 1.6; }   /* ✔ each element: own font-size × 1.6 */
/* h1 at 40px gets 64px lines; p at 16px gets 25.6px lines — perfect */

body { line-height: 24px; }  /* ✘ every child inherits rigid 24px */
/* h1 at 40px squeezed into 24px lines — letters collide! */
Table 40 — Line-height recipes
Textline-heightWhy
Body paragraphs1.5–1.7Reading comfort
Headlines1.1–1.25Tight display look
Buttons/small UI1 + paddingPadding controls the height, not lines

Building a type scale (copy this system)

CODE  ·  A complete professional type system
:root {
  --font-body: "Segoe UI", Arial, sans-serif;
  --text-xs: 0.75rem;   /* 12px badges */
  --text-sm: 0.875rem;  /* 14px captions */
  --text-base: 1rem;    /* 16px body */
  --text-lg: 1.25rem;   /* 20px leads */
  --text-xl: 1.5rem;    /* 24px h3 */
  --text-2xl: 2rem;     /* 32px h2 */
  --text-3xl: 3rem;     /* 48px h1 */
}
body { font-family: var(--font-body); font-size: var(--text-base); line-height: 1.6; }
h1 { font-size: var(--text-3xl); line-height: 1.1; font-weight: 800; }
h2 { font-size: var(--text-2xl); line-height: 1.2; font-weight: 700; }
.lead { font-size: var(--text-lg); font-weight: 300; }
Exercise 13 — Type detective

A site uses body { font-size: 14px; line-height: 20px; } and .card { height: 180px; width: 500px; }. List 4 problems and fixes.

Solution

(1) px font-size ignores user settings → 1rem-based sizes. (2) px line-height squashes big headings → unitless 1.6. (3) fixed height overflows wrapped text → min-height. (4) fixed 500px width breaks 375px phones → width: 100%; max-width: 500px.

Color formats (learn all three, prefer two)

Table 41 — Color formats
FormatExampleBest when
HEX#2563eb, #fffCopying exact brand colors (short, universal)
RGB(A)rgb(37 99 235 / 0.8)Needing transparency (alpha 0–1)
HSL(A)hsl(221 83% 53%)Designing: tweak hue/saturation/lightness intuitively

CODE  ·  Colors in practice
:root {
  --brand: #2563eb;                    /* hex: the brand anchor */
  --brand-soft: rgb(37 99 235 / 0.1);  /* 10% tint for backgrounds */
  --brand-dark: hsl(221 83% 40%);      /* darker shade by lowering lightness */
}
.btn { background: var(--brand); color: #fff; }
.btn:hover { background: var(--brand-dark); }
Pro tip — Design with HSL

Need a hover shade? Keep hue/saturation, lower lightness by 10%. Need a palette? Keep saturation/lightness, rotate hue. HEX can't think like that — HSL is a designer's format.

The contrast law (non-negotiable)

Text must contrast with its background: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18px+). Grey-on-white (#999 on #fff = 2.8:1) fails and excludes millions of users.

Try it yourself — Check contrast in 30 seconds

DevTools → select text → Styles → click the color square → the contrast ratio + pass/fail appears. Fix failures by darkening text or the background until AA passes.

  background-repeat: no-repeat;
  background-position: right top;
  background-size: 200px;
}
/* Gradients are images too — stack them */
.hero {
  background:
    linear-gradient(rgb(11 16 38 / 0.7), rgb(11 16 38 / 0.7)),
    url("../images/hero.webp") center / cover no-repeat;
  color: #fff;
}
.gold-text {
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, #c9a227, #f6e27a);
  -webkit-background-clip: text; background-clip: text; color: transparent;
}

ValueEffect

200px / 50%Exact size

Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Elegant UI = subtle shadows (low alpha, big blur), generous radius (8–16px cards, 999px pills), and ONE brand color with HSL-derived shades. Loud shadows and 6 random colors scream "beginner".

Quick check — Best hover-darkening method?

  2. Lower HSL lightness ~10%
  3. Add black text

Exercise 14 — Style a pricing card

White card, 16px radius, soft shadow, brand-blue price text (3rem/800), grey features list, gold "Popular" pill badge on top. Then add hover: lift 4px + deeper shadow.

display: how elements occupy space

Table 44 — display values
ValueBehaviorWidth/height?Example
blockFull-width row, stacks verticallyYesdiv, p, h1, section
inlineFlows inside text, no breaksNO (ignored!)span, a, strong
inline-blockFlows inline BUT accepts sizesYesButtons, badges, nav items
noneRemoved from page AND from screen readers—Hidden panels, JS toggles
flex / gridLayout engines (next chapters)—Modern layouts
CODE  ·  display fixes juniors google daily
/* Center an image (images are inline by default!) */
img.center { display: block; margin: 0 auto; }
/* Nav items in a row */
.menu li { display: inline-block; }
/* Truly hide vs invisibly keep space vs fade */
.gone { display: none; }              /* removed: layout collapses, readers skip */
.invisible { visibility: hidden; }    /* gap stays, clicks dead, readers vary */
.faded { opacity: 0; }                /* gap stays, STILL clickable! */
Warning — opacity: 0 is NOT hidden

An opacity: 0 button still receives clicks and Tab focus — users click "nothing". For real hiding use display: none (or hidden attribute); for fade animations combine opacity + visibility/pointer-events.

position: the five modes

Table 45 — position modes
ModePositioned relative toScrolls?Use for
staticNormal flow (default)Yes95% of elements — leave it
relativeIts own normal spotYesNudging + becoming an anchor for absolute children
absoluteNearest positioned ancestorWith ancestorBadges, tooltips, overlays inside cards
fixedThe viewport (window)NO (stays)Sticky headers, chat buttons, cookie bars
stickyScrolls until threshold, then sticksHybridSection headers, table of contents
CODE  ·  Positioning patterns
/* Badge pinned to a card corner */
.card { position: relative; }
.card .badge { position: absolute; top: 12px; right: 12px; }
/* Always-visible chat button */
.chat { position: fixed; bottom: 20px; right: 20px; z-index: 50; }
/* Section title that sticks while reading */
.toc { position: sticky; top: 0; background: #fff; }
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Absolute positions against the nearest ancestor with position ≠ static. No positioned ancestor? It flies to the page root — the classic "my badge is in the wrong corner" bug. Fix: position: relative on the intended parent (no offsets needed).

z-index and stacking (why overlaps misbehave)

z-index only works on positioned elements (or flex/grid children). Higher number = closer to viewer. But stacking contexts trap children: a child with z-index: 9999 can NEVER escape above an uncle if its parent created a lower context (via position+z-index, opacity<1, transform, filter…).

Try it yourself — Debug overlaps (2 minutes)

Overlapping wrong? In DevTools inspect both elements: check who is positioned, compare z-indexes, then walk UP parents looking for opacity, transform or z-index creating a trapping context. Fix by restructuring, not by adding more 9s.

CODE  ·  Sane z-index scale (define once)
:root { --z-base: 1; --z-nav: 50; --z-modal: 100; --z-toast: 200; }
.site-nav { position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: var(--z-nav); }

Centering cookbook (stop googling these)

CODE  ·  Every centering recipe
/* Inline content inside a block */
.center-text { text-align: center; }
/* A block with known width */
.box { width: 600px; margin: 0 auto; }   /* max-width version: Ch 14 */
/* Absolute dead-center (unknown size) */
.overlay { position: absolute; top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%); }
/* Flexbox one-liner (Ch 17): the modern answer to everything */
.stage { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; min-height: 60vh; }
Quick check — Badge with position:absolute lands at page corner. Cause?
  1. Wrong z-index
  2. No positioned ancestor — parent needs position:relative
  3. Missing display
  4. Browser bug
Answer: B  ·  Absolute anchors to the nearest positioned ancestor; static parents don't count.
Exercise 15 — Build a product card

Card with image, discount badge top-right (-20%), title, price, "Add" button. Badge must stay glued to the card on all screen sizes.

Solution

.card{position:relative} .badge{position:absolute;top:12px;right:12px} + image display:block;width:100%. Test: resize the window — the badge rides with the card because its anchor IS the card.

Elzero CSS FlexboxGamal FlexboxAngela §Flex

Mental model: container, items, two axes

main axis (justify-content) ----------------------------------> +------------------------------------------------------------+ | [Item 1] [Item 2] [Item 3] | +------------------------------------------------------------+ cross axis (align-items) runs vertically (top to bottom) flex-direction: column swaps them: main = vertical, cross = horizontal
Figure 9 — Flexbox axes (flex-direction: row)

The parent (container) gets display: flex and controls alignment; children (items) control their own growth.

CODE  ·  Your first flexbox (perfect centering + navbar)
.center-stage { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; min-height: 50vh; }
.navbar { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; gap: 16px; }

Container properties (set on parent)

Table 46 — Flex container cheat-sheet
PropertyValuesJob
display: flex—Activates flexbox for direct children
flex-directionrow (default) / column / row-reverseMain-axis direction
justify-contentflex-start, center, flex-end, space-between, space-around, space-evenly, gapSpacing along MAIN axis
align-itemsstretch, flex-start, center, flex-end, baselineAlignment along CROSS axis
flex-wrapnowrap / wrapAllow multiple lines (responsive rows!)
gap16px (or row-gap column-gap)Gutters WITHOUT margin hacks
Warning — space-between vs space-evenly

space-between: first/last glued to edges, gaps only inside. space-around: half-gaps at edges. space-evenly: all gaps (including edges) perfectly equal. Pick deliberately — screenshots reveal the wrong one instantly.

Item properties (set on children)

Table 47 — Flex item cheat-sheet
PropertyExampleJob
flex-grow1Share of EXTRA space (0 = none)
flex-shrink0Refuse to shrink (1 = shrink normally)
flex-basis250pxStarting size before growing/shrinking
flex1 1 250pxShorthand: grow shrink basis (flex: 1 = grow fully)
align-selfcenterOverride cross-axis alignment for THIS item only
order-1Visual order (DOM order unchanged — careful with screen readers!)
CODE  ·  The holy-grail sidebar layout in 6 lines
.layout { display: flex; gap: 24px; }
.sidebar { flex: 0 0 260px; }   /* fixed 260px, never grows/shrinks */
.content { flex: 1; }            /* eats all remaining space */
Think of it like this — flex-grow is sharing pizza

Three items with flex-grow: 1, 2, 1 split leftover space like 4 pizza slices: 1, 2, 1. flex-shrink: 0 is saying "never take MY slice" when space runs out. flex-basis is the plate size you start with.

Five classic patterns (memorize these)

CODE  ·  Pattern 1 — Navbar: logo left, links right
.nav { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; }
CODE  ·  Pattern 2 — Card row that wraps on mobile
.cards { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 20px; }
.cards .card { flex: 1 1 260px; }   /* min 260px, grow, wrap as needed */
CODE  ·  Pattern 3 — Media object: thumbnail + text
.media { display: flex; gap: 16px; align-items: flex-start; }
.media img { flex: 0 0 120px; }
CODE  ·  Pattern 4 — Form row: input grows, button fixed
.form-row { display: flex; gap: 8px; }
.form-row input { flex: 1; }
CODE  ·  Pattern 5 — Footer: columns that stack on mobile
.footer { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 32px; }
.footer > * { flex: 1 1 200px; }
Interview question — Flexbox vs Grid — when which?

Expected: "Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts — a row OR a column: navs, card rows, form lines, centering. Grid for two-dimensional — rows AND columns together: page scaffolding, galleries with alignment in both directions. They compose: Grid page + Flexbox components inside."

Quick check — justify-content aligns along…
  1. Always horizontal
  2. The MAIN axis (row→horizontal, column→vertical)
  3. The cross axis
  4. Diagonal
Answer: B  ·  Justify = main axis; the axis direction depends on flex-direction. This answers half of all Flexbox confusion.
Exercise 16 — Pricing table with Flexbox

Three pricing cards in a row (wrap on mobile), middle card highlighted and slightly taller, features list inside each, buttons bottom-aligned across cards.

Solution

.plans{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:24px;align-items:stretch} .plan{flex:1 1 260px;display:flex;flex-direction:column} .plan ul{flex:1} .featured{border:2px solid gold;transform:scale(1.03)} — inner column flex + flex:1 list pushes buttons to equal bottoms.
