Angela §SQLElzero databaseTutorialspoint SQL

Tables, rows, keys (the spreadsheet that enforces rules)

users: id (PK) | email (UNIQUE, NOT NULL) | name | created_at 1 | [email protected] | Sara | 2026-01-02 2 | [email protected] | Omar | 2026-03-11 PK = Primary Key: unique ID per row. FK = Foreign Key: points at another table's PK.
Figure 19 — A users table (columns = schema, rows = data)
CODE  ·  Create tables with real constraints
CREATE TABLE users (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  total INT NOT NULL CHECK (total >= 0),
  status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'
);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id);  -- JOINs stay fast
Table 93 — Constraints (rules the DB enforces FOR you)
ConstraintJob
PRIMARY KEYUnique row ID (indexed automatically)
FOREIGN KEY … REFERENCESMust point at a real row (no orphans!)
UNIQUENo duplicates (emails, usernames)
NOT NULL / DEFAULT / CHECKRequired values, fallbacks, valid ranges

Queries: the daily 90%

CODE  ·  SELECT power tour
SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE email ILIKE '%@x.com' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;
SELECT status, COUNT(*), SUM(total) FROM orders GROUP BY status HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
INSERT INTO users(email, name) VALUES ('[email protected]', 'A') RETURNING id;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = $1;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'abandoned' AND created_at < now() - interval '30 days';
Table 94 — Query clauses in order
ClauseJobExample
WHEREFilter rowsWHERE total > 1000
ORDER BYSort (DESC = biggest first)ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT/OFFSETPage resultsLIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 (page 3)
GROUP BY + aggregatesSummarize groupsCOUNT(*), SUM(total), AVG(total)
HAVINGFilter GROUPS (WHERE can't)HAVING COUNT(*) > 5

JOINs visualized (the fear-killer)

INNER: only matching pairs (users WITH orders) .......... [ overlap only ] LEFT: ALL users + their orders or NULL (find inactive!) .. [ left circle all ] salaries per user: LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY user.
Figure 20 — JOINs as Venn diagrams (users ⟷ orders on user_id)
CODE  ·  JOINs you will actually write
-- Every user with their order count (including 0-order users!)
SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders, COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS spent
FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name ORDER BY spent DESC;

Safe Node access (parameters, never strings!)

CODE  ·  node-postgres with $1 parameters (injection-proof)
import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
const byEmail = async email => {
  const { rows } = await pool.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email]);
  return rows[0] || null;   // $1 = value sent SEPARATELY — never in the SQL text ✔
};
// NEVER: `... WHERE email = '${email}'` — `' OR '1'='1` steals your whole table! (Ch 45)
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

SQL + constraints = data that CANNOT be invalid (uniques, FKs, checks enforced by the engine). Query with JOINs/GROUP BY for answers, paginate everything, and pass values as PARAMETERS — string-built SQL is how databases get stolen.

Quick check — LEFT JOIN users→orders shows…
  1. Only users with orders
  2. ALL users, NULLs where no orders
  3. Only orders
  4. Duplicates
Answer: B  ·  LEFT keeps every left row; unmatched rights become NULL — perfect for "inactive users" reports.
Exercise 39 — Mini shop reports

Schema: products(id, name, price), sales(id, product_id FK, qty, at). Queries: (1) revenue per product, (2) unsold products, (3) top day by revenue. All parameterized from Node.

Solution

(1) LEFT JOIN + SUM(price*qty) GROUP BY product. (2) same + HAVING COUNT(sales.id)=0 (or WHERE sales.id IS NULL). (3) GROUP BY date_trunc('day', at) ORDER BY SUM DESC LIMIT 1. Reports = JOIN + GROUP + aggregates, always.

Documents: JSON that persists

Figure 21 — Same blog post: SQL (3 tables + JOINs) vs Mongo (1 document)
CODE  ·  Mongoose schema = flexible structure + validation (npm i mongoose)
import mongoose from "mongoose";
const postSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  title: { type: String, required: true, trim: true, maxlength: 140 },
  slug: { type: String, required: true, unique: true, index: true },
  tags: { type: [String], default: [] },
  author: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: "User", required: true },
  comments: [{ by: String, text: { type: String, maxlength: 1000 }, at: { type: Date, default: Date.now } }]
}, { timestamps: true });   // createdAt + updatedAt free ✔
export const Post = mongoose.model("Post", postSchema);

CRUD + queries

CODE  ·  Daily Mongoose operations
await Post.create({ title: "Hi", slug: "hi", author: userId });
await Post.find({ tags: "js" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20).populate("author", "name");
await Post.updateOne({ slug }, { $set: { title } });
await Post.deleteOne({ slug });
// Operators: { price: { $gte: 100, $lt: 500 } }, { $or: [{a}, {b}] }

OperatorJob

Embed vs reference (the design decision)

Table 96 — Embed or reference?
Embed (nest inside)Reference (ObjectId + populate)
Read together always (post + comments)Independent life (users, products)
Bounded growth (dozens, not millions)Unbounded growth (all orders ever)
No cross-parent queriesQueried across parents

  user: { type: ObjectId, ref: "User", required: true, index: true },

  total: { type: Number, min: 0 }
});
await Order.findById(id).populate("user", "name email").populate("items.product", "name price");

SQL vs NoSQL (the honest guide)

Table 97 — Decision matrix
NeedWinnerWhy
Money, inventory (must never corrupt)PostgreSQLACID transactions + constraints enforce truth
Flexible content, fast iterationMongoDBSchema evolves without migrations
Complex relations + reportsPostgreSQLJOINs + GROUP BY are unmatched
Huge write streams, simple readsMongoDBScales horizontally with ease
Interview question — SQL or NoSQL for an e-commerce site?

Expected: "Both, split by job: PostgreSQL for orders/payments/inventory where consistency is money; MongoDB (or similar) for catalogs/reviews/activity feeds where shape varies and reads dominate. Decide per BOUNDED CONTEXT, not per company." Dogmatism either way = junior signal.

Exercise 40 — Catalog + orders hybrid

Design: Mongo Product (variants embedded, reviews embedded capped at 50 + overflow note) + SQL orders (FK to users, totals CHECK ≥ 0). Justify each choice in 3 sentences + write both schemas.

Solution

Products vary wildly (sizes/colors/specs) and render as one page → embed in Mongo. Orders move money and join users/reports → SQL constraints + transactions. Overflow: keep latest 50 reviews embedded + reviewCount + separate query for full history (bounded growth rule).

Authentication — Passwords, Sessions and JWT

Advanced~ 130 min
Register/login flows, bcrypt hashing, sessions vs tokens, and protected routes.
In this chapter
  • Auth vs authz (know the difference!)
  • bcrypt hashing + salts
  • Sessions (cookies) vs JWT
  • Access + refresh rotation
  • Protecting Express routes
Angela §AuthElzero authMDN security

Authentication vs authorization (say it right)

Table 98 — The two words interviews test
WordQuestionExample
Authentication (authN)WHO are you?Login with email + password
Authorization (authZ)WHAT may you do?Only admins delete users
CODE  ·  The golden auth rules (memorize all five)
1. NEVER store plain passwords — bcrypt hashes ONLY (cost factor 12)
2. NEVER roll your own crypto — use bcrypt + jsonwebtoken + platform TLS
3. NEVER put secrets in JWT payloads — payloads are READABLE (signed, not encrypted!)
4. Tokens in HttpOnly cookies (XSS-proof) — NOT localStorage (XSS-readable!)
5. ALWAYS HTTPS in production — tokens over HTTP are postcards, not letters

Passwords with bcrypt (the only way)

CODE  ·  Register + login (npm i bcrypt jsonwebtoken)
import bcrypt from "bcrypt";
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

// REGISTER: hash, never store plain ✔
const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12);   // 12 = cost factor (~250ms)
await User.create({ email, passwordHash: hash });

// LOGIN: compare (timing-safe) — same message either way (no user enumeration!)
const user = await User.findOne({ email });
const ok = user && await bcrypt.compare(password, user.passwordHash);
if (!ok) return res.status(401).json({ error: { message: "Invalid email or password" } });
Think of it like this — Hashing is a meat grinder (one-way)

Beef (password) → mince (hash) is easy; mince → beef is impossible. Salts (bcrypt auto-adds) mean identical passwords get DIFFERENT hashes — rainbow tables (pre-ground beef dictionaries) become useless. Cost factor = grinder slowness: slow for attackers, fine for logins.

Sessions vs JWT (the architecture choice)

Table 99 — Sessions (stateful) vs JWT (stateless)
Sessions + HttpOnly cookieJWT access + refresh
Server memoryStores session IDs (Redis/DB)Stores nothing (verifies signature)
RevokeInstant (delete session)Needs denylist/short expiry
ScaleShared store requiredAny server verifies (secret/public key)
Best forMonoliths, instant-revoke needsAPIs, mobile, microservices
CODE  ·  JWT pair + rotation (15-min access, 7-day refresh in HttpOnly cookie)
const access = jwt.sign({ sub: user.id, role: user.role }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: "15m" });
const refresh = jwt.sign({ sub: user.id, v: user.tokenVersion }, process.env.REFRESH_SECRET, { expiresIn: "7d" });
res.cookie("refresh", refresh, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "strict", maxAge: 7*864e5 });
res.json({ data: { access } });   // access in memory (JS var), refresh in cookie ✔

// Logout EVERYWHERE: bump tokenVersion → all refresh tokens die instantly
CODE  ·  Protecting routes (middleware reads access token)
function requireAuth(req, res, next) {
  const token = req.headers.authorization?.replace("Bearer ", "");
  if (!token) return next({ status: 401, message: "Login required" });
  try {
    req.user = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);  // throws if bad/expired
    next();
  } catch { next({ status: 401, message: "Session expired — please log in" }); }
}
const requireRole = role => (req, res, next) =>
  req.user?.role === role ? next() : next({ status: 403, message: "Admins only" });
app.delete("/api/v1/users/:id", requireAuth, requireRole("admin"), handler);
Warning — JWT payload is PUBLIC

Anyone can base64-decode {sub, role} — it proves AUTHENTICITY (signature), not secrecy. Never put passwords, emails-you-hide, or internals inside. Secrets stay server-side, referenced by ID.

Interview question — Where do you store JWTs and why?

Expected: "Access token in memory, refresh token in HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie. Never localStorage — any XSS steals it. Short access expiry limits damage; refresh rotation + token versioning enables instant global logout." Mention CSRF+SameSite interplay (next chapter) = senior.

Quick check — Same login error for bad email AND bad password because…
  1. Laziness
  2. Prevents user enumeration (attackers can't harvest registered emails)
  3. Faster
  4. Required by JWT
Answer: B  ·  Distinct messages ("no such user" vs "wrong password") let attackers probe your user list. Uniform 401s close the oracle.
Exercise 41 — Full auth slice

Register (validate + unique email + bcrypt) → login (uniform 401) → /me (requireAuth) → admin-only DELETE (requireRole) → logout-all (tokenVersion bump). Test: expired access (401), user hitting admin route (403), refresh after logout-all (dead).

Solution

Covered above end-to-end; add tests for each code path. Verify cookies flags in DevTools Application tab (HttpOnly ✔ Secure ✔ SameSite=Strict ✔). Auth done = boring, uniform, and strict.

Think like an attacker (trust boundaries)

[browser] --input--> [API] --query--> [DB] --data--> [browser renders] ^ ^ ^ ^ XSS here validate here inject here escape here RULE: validate at ENTRY, parameterize at QUERY, escape at RENDER. Every layer, every time.
Figure 22 — Every arrow crossing is an attack surface

XSS: your site running attacker code

Table 100 — XSS flavors
TypeHowExample
StoredMalicious post saved, runs for every readerComment with <img onerror=steal()>
ReflectedPayload in URL, server echoes itSearch page echoing ?q=<script>…
DOMClient JS sinks user data into HTMLel.innerHTML = location.hash
CODE  ·  Defenses (layered — use ALL)
// 1. Render safely: textContent/createElement for user data (Ch 29!) ✔
// 2. Sanitize rich HTML server-side (allowlist tags/attrs) if HTML input is required
// 3. Content-Security-Policy header: only YOUR scripts run (inline attacker code dies)
app.use(helmet.contentSecurityPolicy({
  directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"], scriptSrc: ["'self'"], imgSrc: ["'self'", "data:"] }
}));
// 4. HttpOnly cookies: stolen XSS still can't read tokens (Ch 44!) ✔

CSRF: hijacking the logged-in browser

Victim logged into bank.com visits evil.com, whose hidden form POSTs to bank.com/transfer — the browser ATTACHES cookies automatically. Defense layers:

Table 101 — CSRF defenses
DefenseHow
SameSite=Strict/Lax cookiesBrowser withholds cookies on cross-site requests (primary defense!)
CSRF tokensServer-issued per-form secret, verified on mutation
Custom headers + CORSAPIs requiring Authorization/JSON preflight block simple forged forms
GET never mutatesTransfers/deletes are POST/DELETE (browsers prefetch GETs!)

Injection: queries built from strings

CODE  ·  NEVER build queries from strings (both databases!)
// SQL — parameterized ✔ vs string ✘:
pool.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email]);  // ✔ safe
// `... WHERE email = '${email}'`  // ✘ ' OR '1'='1 steals all rows!

// Mongo — operators from user input are poison:
User.find({ email: req.body.email });              // body {email: {"$ne": null}} matches ALL!
const email = String(req.body.email || "");        // force scalar ✔
User.find({ email });                              // safe
Table 102 — Injection family (same disease, many organs)
TargetPoisonCure
SQL' OR '1'='1Parameterized queries ($1, ?)
NoSQL{"$ne": null} objectsType-check scalars; schema validation
Commands; rm -rf in filenamesNever shell out with input; allowlist chars
Paths../../etc/passwdbasename + allowlist + uuid renames (Ch 41)
HTML/JS<script>, onerror=Escape output + CSP + textContent

Hardening stack (copy this)

CODE  ·  Production security middleware (npm i helmet express-rate-limit)
import helmet from "helmet";
import rateLimit from "express-rate-limit";
app.use(helmet());   // secure headers: HSTS, noSniff, frameguard, CSP…
app.use("/api/v1/auth", rateLimit({ windowMs: 15*60e3, max: 20 }));  // brute-force killer
app.use("/api", rateLimit({ windowMs: 15*60e3, max: 300 }));
app.use(express.json({ limit: "100kb" }));       // giant-body killer
Security ship checklist (OWASP-flavored)
  • - bcrypt(12) passwords; uniform login errors; HTTPS everywhere; HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookies
  • - All inputs validated; all queries parameterized; all user HTML escaped/sanitized + CSP
  • - Auth on every private route; role checks server-side (never trust client claims!)
  • - Rate limits on auth + API; body caps; security headers via helmet
  • - Secrets in env only; npm audit clean; errors never leak stacks; logs never include secrets/tokens
  • - Backups tested (restore rehearsal!) + dependency updates scheduled
Interview question — Your top 3 web vulnerabilities?

Expected: "Injection — parameterized queries and input validation; XSS — safe rendering plus CSP plus HttpOnly cookies; broken auth — bcrypt, short-lived tokens, rotation, and rate-limited login. Then CSRF via SameSite + tokens, and security headers/rate limiting as baseline hygiene." Structured + layered = hired.

Exercise 42 — Red-team your API

Attack your Ch 40–41 API: XSS comment, ' OR 1=1 login, {"$ne":null} body, 50MB upload, 500 rapid logins, forged admin role in JWT. Every attack must fail CLOSED (4xx, no data, no crash) — document each fix.

Solution

Expected results: CSP+escaping neuters XSS; parameters neutralize injection; type checks kill operator objects; caps reject giants (413); rate limit 429s the flood; signature verification rejects forged roles (401). Failed-closed everywhere = shippable.

Thinking in components (Lego UI)

<App> (state lives high, flows down) |-- <Header cartCount={3} /> |-- <ProductList> -- <ProductCard /> x N (props in, events up) +-- <Footer /> RULES: one component = one job; data flows DOWN via props; events bubble UP via callbacks.
Figure 23 — One page = a tree of reusable pieces
CODE  ·  Your first components (Vite: npm create vite@latest shop -- --template react)
function Price({ value }) {                       // props = inputs (read-only!)
  return <strong className="price">${value}</strong>;
}
function ProductCard({ product, onAdd }) {
  return (
    <article className="card">
      <h3>{product.name}</h3>
      <Price value={product.price} />
      <button onClick={() => onAdd(product.id)}>Add to cart</button>
    </article>
  );
}
Table 103 — JSX rules (HTML with 3 twists)
RuleExampleWhy
className not class<div className="x">class is a JS keyword
{} injects JS<h1>{user.name}</h1>Any expression: vars, maps, ternaries
One parent<>…</> fragmentsComponents return ONE root
onClick={fn}camelCase + function refNOT strings: onClick={() => add(id)}

State: useState + events

CODE  ·  State = data that re-renders when changed
import { useState } from "react";
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);      // [value, setter]
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>Clicked {count}×</button>;
}
// ARRAY/OBJECT state: replace, never mutate! (Ch 28 immutability pays off)
const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);
const add = id => setCart(prev => [...prev, id]);
const remove = id => setCart(prev => prev.filter(x => x !== id));
Warning — State mutation = silent UI death

cart.push(id); setCart(cart) keeps the SAME array reference — React sees "nothing changed" and skips rendering. Always create NEW arrays/objects ([...prev], filter, map). The #1 React beginner bug, inherited straight from Ch 24's references lesson.

Lists, keys, conditional UI

CODE  ·  The three rendering patterns
function ProductList({ items, loading, error, onAdd }) {
  if (loading) return <p>Loading…</p>;              // 1. early returns per state (Ch 33!)
  if (error) return <p>Failed: {error} <button>Retry</button></p>;
  if (!items.length) return <p>No products yet.</p>; // 2. empty state ✔
  return (
    <ul>{items.map(p => (
      <li key={p.id}><ProductCard product={p} onAdd={onAdd} /></li>  // 3. key = stable id
    ))}</ul>
  );
}
// Inline conditions: {isAdmin && <AdminPanel />} ··· {count > 0 ? <Cart/> : <Empty/>}

Effects: useEffect + data fetching

CODE  ·  Fetch on mount, cleanup on unmount (Ch 32–33 patterns, React-flavored)
import { useState, useEffect } from "react";
function useProducts() {
  const [data, setData] = useState([]);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState("loading");
  useEffect(() => {
    const ctrl = new AbortController();            // cleanup cancels flight ✔
    (async () => {
      try {
        const res = await fetch("https://dummyjson.com/products?limit=12", { signal: ctrl.signal });
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        setData((await res.json()).products); setStatus("ready");
      } catch (e) { if (e.name !== "AbortError") setStatus("error"); }
    })();
    return () => ctrl.abort();                     // unmount/StrictMode safety
  }, []);                                          // [] = run ONCE
  return { data, status };
}
Table 104 — useEffect dependency array
ArrayRunsClassic bug
[]Once on mountForgetting needed deps (stale data)
[id]On mount + when id changesMissing dep = stale closure!
(no array)After EVERY renderAccidental infinite fetch loops

useRef + routing idea + cart project

CODE  ·  Refs hold non-render values (timers, DOM nodes, previous values)
import { useRef, useEffect } from "react";
function Search({ onSearch }) {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);
  useEffect(() => inputRef.current.focus(), []);   // autofocus on mount
  return <input ref={inputRef} onChange={e => onSearch(e.target.value)} />;
}
// Routing (npm i react-router-dom): URL ↔ component map
// <Routes><Route path="/" element={<Shop/>} /><Route path="/cart" element={<Cart/>} /></Routes>
CODE  ·  Mini project — shop with cart (state lifted to App)
function App() {
  const { data: products, status } = useProducts();
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);
  const add = id => setCart(p => [...p, id]);
  const total = cart.reduce((s, id) => s + (products.find(p => p.id === id)?.price || 0), 0);
  return (<>
    <Header count={cart.length} total={total} />
    <ProductList items={products} loading={status === "loading"}
      error={status === "error" ? "Load failed" : ""} onAdd={add} />
  </>);
}
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

React = components (UI Lego) + props (down) + state (owned data) + effects (outside world). Lift shared state UP to the lowest common parent; derive (totals, counts) instead of storing; fetch in effects with cleanup. Everything else is practice.

Interview question — Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs?

Expected: "Controlled: value + onChange in state — React owns the truth (validation, disable logic, instant feedback). Uncontrolled: refs read DOM on demand — simpler for one-shot forms. Default to controlled; reach for refs for focus/file inputs." Then note keys must be stable IDs.

Exercise 43 — Reactify the expense tracker

Rebuild Ch 35's tracker in React: useState items + localStorage effect (load once, save on change) + derived totals + category bars. Same architecture triangle — compare line counts with the vanilla version.

Solution

const [items, setItems] = useState(() => load("exp", [])); useEffect(() => save("exp", items), [items]); — persistence becomes 2 lines. Totals via reduce during render (derived, never stored). ~40% less DOM code than vanilla: React owns rendering, you own data.

Beyond useState: Zustand + Redux Toolkit (global state grows up)

Context broadcasts to every consumer on every change — fine for themes, painful for carts updated 60×/second. Dedicated stores update ONLY the components that read the changed slice.

CODE  ·  Zustand (npm i zustand) — global state in 10 lines
import { create } from "zustand";
export const useCart = create(set => ({
  items: [],
  add: id => set(s => ({ items: [...s.items, id] })),
  clear: () => set({ items: [] })
}));
// Any component, zero providers:
const items = useCart(s => s.items);   // re-renders ONLY when items change ✔
const add = useCart(s => s.add);
Table 105 — useState vs Context vs Zustand vs Redux Toolkit
NeedPickWhy
Local (form, toggle)useState/useReducerSimplest, co-located
Slow + global (theme, user)ContextBuilt-in, no deps
Fast + global (cart, player)ZustandSliced subscriptions, tiny API
Huge teams + time-travelRedux ToolkitDevTools, conventions, middleware
```jsx:Redux Toolkit slice (the 80% pattern: createSlice + configureStore)
// store/cartSlice.js
import { createSlice } from "@reduxjs/toolkit";
const slice = createSlice({ name: "cart", initialState: [],
reducers: { add: (s, a) => { s.push(a.payload); }, clear: () => [] } });
export const { add, clear } = slice.actions;
export default slice.reducer;
// Component: const items = useSelector(s => s.cart); const d = useDispatch(); d(add(id));
```
::: interview Context vs Redux?
Expected: "Context is a broadcast pipe, not a state manager — every update re-renders all consumers. I use Context for slow global state, Zustand for fast slices, Redux Toolkit when the team needs DevTools conventions and middleware. I can show the re-render difference in DevTools Profiler." Trade-offs + proof = senior.

React performance checklist (measure, then memo)

The 7-step React speed pass (in order!)
  • - Profiler FIRST: record the interaction, fix the widest bars (no blind memo!)
  • - Keys stable (ids!) + lists windowed (virtualize 500+ rows)
  • - State pushed DOWN (a typing input shouldn't re-render the page!)
  • - Expensive derived data in useMemo; callbacks in useCallback ONLY when passed to memo'd children
  • - Routes lazy (lazy(() => import()) + Suspense) — ship 30KB, not 300KB
  • - Images: next/image or sized AVIF + lazy (Ch 61!)
  • - Context split (Auth/Cart/Theme separate) + values memoized
CODE  ·  Lazy routes (the biggest single win, 3 lines)
import { lazy, Suspense } from "react";
const Admin = lazy(() => import("./Admin.js"));
<Suspense fallback={<p>Loading…</p>}><Admin /></Suspense>

Solution

Typical kills: search input re-rendering 500 cards (push query state into the list component + memo rows), monolith context (split!), admin in main bundle (lazy → −120KB). Before/after flame graphs side by side = interview gold.

Advanced Selectors — :has, :is, :where and Pseudo Power

:has() — style parents by children (the revolution)

CODE  ·  Parent-aware styling (no JS!)
/* Cards containing images get padding-free tops */
.card:has(> img) { padding-top: 0; }
/* Forms flag errors upward */
form:has(input:invalid) .submit-hint { display: block; }
/* Nav highlights when dropdown open */
nav:has(.dropdown:hover) { background: navy; }
/* Quantity queries: grids adapt to count */
.grid:has(> :nth-child(5)) { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }
Warning — :has() performance

:has() can be expensive over huge trees — scope it (.card:has(…) not *:has(…)), and never chain multiple :has() on hot paths like table rows.

:is() vs :where() (specificity weapons)

CODE  ·  Same matching, different scores
/* :is() takes the STRONGEST argument's specificity */
:is(h1, .title, #hero) { … }   /* scores 1-0-0 (the ID!) — dangerous */
/* :where() scores ZERO always — perfect for resets/defaults */
:where(h1, h2, p, ul) { margin: 0; }   /* 0-0-0: any class overrides ✔ */
/* Forgiving parsing: unknown selectors inside don't kill the rule */
:is(.a, :bogus, .b) { … }   /* works! plain lists would die entirely */

nth patterns + generated content

CODE  ·  Position patterns professionals use
tbody tr:nth-child(even) { background: #f6f8fc; }  /* zebra */
.gallery > :nth-child(3n) { margin-right: 0; }     /* every 3rd */
li:nth-child(n+4) { … }    /* 4th onward */  li:nth-child(-n+3) { … } /* first 3 */
li:only-child { … }        /* lonely items */  :empty { … } /* truly empty */

::marker { color: gold; font-size: 1.2em; }
::selection { background: #c9a227; color: #111; }
.article::first-letter { font-size: 3em; float: left; line-height: 1; }
a[href^="http"]::after { content: " (" attr(href) ")"; font-size: .8em; }  /* print URLs! */

Masks, clips and blend reveals

CODE  ·  Visibility art direction

  background: linear-gradient(90deg, #c9a227, #fff, #c9a227);
  -webkit-background-clip: text; background-clip: text; color: transparent;
}
.fade-list { mask-image: linear-gradient(black 75%, transparent); }  /* soft list end */
.img-duo { filter: grayscale(1) contrast(1.1); mix-blend-mode: multiply; }  /* print duotone */
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Backgrounds are a STACK (comma layers), gradients are IMAGES (anywhere url() works), masks control VISIBILITY, blend modes control MIXING. Compose the four and "CSS art" stops being magic.

Chapter 52

Modern JavaScript Deep — Map, Set, Iterators and More

Advanced~ 100 min
The ES6+ tools seniors reach for daily: proper collections, lazy sequences and clean async iteration.
In this chapter

Elzero advancedMDNGamal JS

Map vs Object, Set vs Array (choose right)

Table 118 — The decision tables
NeedUseWhy
String keys + JSON + literalsObject {}Ergonomics, JSON-native
ANY keys (objects, functions) + order + sizeMapmap.size, insertion order, no prototype traps
Unique values / dedupe / membershipSetO(1) has(), auto-unique
CODE  ·  Collections doing real jobs
// 1. Dedupe + count in two lines
const tags = ["js", "css", "js", "html"];
const unique = [...new Set(tags)];                    // ["js","css","html"]
// 2. Frequency map
const freq = new Map();
for (const t of tags) freq.set(t, (freq.get(t) || 0) + 1);
// 3. Object-keyed cache (impossible with {})
const prices = new Map();
prices.set(productObj, 1299);                         // keys can be OBJECTS ✔
// 4. WeakMap private-ish + GC-friendly metadata
const meta = new WeakMap();
meta.set(user, { lastSeen: Date.now() });             // vanishes when user GC'd ✔
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Object for RECORDS (known string keys, JSON). Map for DICTIONARIES (dynamic/any keys, frequent add/delete). Set for UNIQUENESS. WeakMap/WeakSet for metadata that must not leak memory.

Generators: lazy power

CODE  ·  Sequences without arrays (infinite + paged data)
// Infinite IDs, zero memory
function* ids(prefix = "u_") { let n = 1; while (true) yield `${prefix}${n++}`; }
const gen = ids(); gen.next().value;   // "u_1" (pauses until next()!)

// Paginate an API lazily — consumers just loop
async function* allPages(fetchPage) {
  let page = 1;
  while (true) {
    const { items, hasMore } = await fetchPage(page++);
    yield* items;                       // delegate each item
    if (!hasMore) return;
  }
}
for await (const user of allPages(p => api(`/users?page=${p}`))) { paint(user); }
Think of it like this — Generators are pause buttons

A normal function runs to the end. A generator PAUSES at every yield and resumes on next() — producing values on demand. Infinite sequences, huge files, paged APIs: all become simple loops.

Quick check — [...new Set([1,1,2])] =
  1. [1,1,2]
  2. [1,2]
  3. Set{1,2}
  4. Error
Answer: B  ·  Set drops duplicates; spread converts back to array. The one-line dedupe.
Exercise 50 — LRU cache with Map

LRU(limit) with get/set; Map insertion order = age; get refreshes (delete+set); set evicts oldest when full. O(1) everything.

Solution

class LRU{constructor(n){this.n=n;this.m=new Map()}get(k){if(!this.m.has(k))return;const v=this.m.get(k);this.m.delete(k);this.m.set(k,v);return v}set(k,v){if(this.m.has(k))this.m.delete(k);this.m.set(k,v);if(this.m.size>this.n)this.m.delete(this.m.keys().next().value)}} — Map order does the bookkeeping.

Chapter 53

Design Patterns — Module, Factory, Observer, Singleton

Advanced~ 110 min
Four battle-tested solutions to recurring problems — with honest "when NOT to use" notes.
In this chapter
  • Module (encapsulation)
  • Factory (configurable creation)
  • Observer (events at scale)
  • Singleton (one shared thing)
  • Anti-pattern warnings
Elzero patternsMDNInterview

1. Module (ESM + closures)

CODE  ·  Private-by-default features (Ch 26 closures + Ch 28 modules, combined)
// cart.js — state NOBODY can corrupt, API everyone uses
const items = [];
export const add = p => items.push(p);
export const total = () => items.reduce((s, p) => s + p.price, 0);
export const list = () => [...items];   // copy out — never the live array!

2. Factory (one maker, many configs)

CODE  ·  Configured creators beat option-soup constructors
const makeApi = base => (path, opts) =>
  fetch(base + path, { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, ...opts })
    .then(r => { if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status}`); return r.json(); });
const shopApi = makeApi("https://shop.example/api");
const authApi = makeApi("https://auth.example/");
await shopApi("/products");   // preconfigured, tiny call sites ✔

3. Observer (pub/sub at scale)

CODE  ·  Tiny event bus — decoupled features (cart ↔ badge ↔ toast)
const bus = new Map();
export const on = (ev, fn) => { (bus.get(ev) ?? bus.set(ev, new Set()).get(ev)).add(fn); };
export const emit = (ev, data) => bus.get(ev)?.forEach(fn => fn(data));
// cart.js: emit("cart:add", item) ··· badge.js: on("cart:add", updateCount)

4. Singleton (exactly one)

CODE  ·  One DB pool / one config / one logger — module instances ARE singletons
// db.js
import pg from "pg";
export const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
// Every importer shares THE pool (modules evaluate once) ✔ — no class ceremony needed.
Table 119 — Pattern honesty table (when NOT to)
PatternSkip when
ModuleSingle-use script (functions + file scope suffice)
FactoryOne configuration exists (YAGNI!)
ObserverTwo modules + one event (direct call is clearer)
SingletonTests need isolation (inject instead) or state should be per-request
Interview question — Singleton in Node.js?

Expected: "ES modules evaluate once and export live bindings — so an exported instance IS the singleton. For per-request state (tests, tenants) I export a factory instead." Practical + honest beats textbook recitation.

Exercise 51 — Theme bus + store

Mini-store: createStore(init) with get/set/subscribe (observer); theme + cart as two stores; header/cart/toast subscribe. No framework, ~30 lines, React's useSyncExternalStore-compatible shape.

Solution

const createStore=v=>{const s=new Set();return{get:()=>v,set:n=>{v=n;s.forEach(f=>f(v))},sub:f=>(s.add(f),()=>s.delete(f))}} — get/set/sub triple. Unsubscribe fn returned = leak-free effects.

The bug-cost curve (why bother)

dev writes test .......... $1 (seconds) code review finds ........ $10 (minutes) QA finds ................. $100 (hours) production incident ...... $10,000+ (outage + trust) Tests move discovery LEFT — cheapest possible moment.

CODE  ·  Your first test (npm i -D vitest; script: "test": "vitest")

  it("adds positives", () => expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5));

Table 120 — Assertions that matter (90% of tests)
MatcherChecks
toBePrimitives (Object.is)

toContain / toMatchSubstring/regex/array membership
toThrowErrorexpect(() => fn()).toThrow("msg")

Mocking: fetch, time, randomness

CODE  ·  Control the uncontrollable
import { vi, it, expect, beforeEach } from "vitest";
// 1. Mock fetch (never hit real APIs in unit tests!)
global.fetch = vi.fn(async () => ({ ok: true, json: async () => [{ id: 1 }] }));
// 2. Mock time (debounce/timers without waiting!)
vi.useFakeTimers();
debounced("x"); vi.advanceTimersByTime(300); expect(fetch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
// 3. Mock randomness/UUIDs (deterministic snapshots)
vi.spyOn(crypto, "randomUUID").mockReturnValue("fixed-id");
CODE  ·  Testing DOM + async (happy-dom + Testing-Library style)
// npm i -D happy-dom @testing-library/dom
import { getByRole, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/dom";
document.body.innerHTML = `<form><input name="email"><button>Go</button></form>`;
fireEvent.input(screen.getByRole("textbox"), { target: { value: "[email protected]" } });
await fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
expect(document.querySelector(".done")).toBeTruthy();
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Test BEHAVIOR ("submitting valid form shows success"), not implementation (not "calls function X"). Pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration, rare E2E. Untested code = legacy code the day after you write it.

The refactor test (why types win)

Rename user.name → user.fullName across 50 files: JS = find-and-hope (miss one = production crash); TS = compiler lists EVERY spot before you run anything. Types are executable documentation + a tireless reviewer.

CODE  ·  Types pay rent immediately
type ID = string;                                   // aliases name concepts
interface User { id: ID; name: string; age?: number }  // ? = optional
function greet(u: User): string { return `Hi ${u.name}`; }
const isAdmin = (u: User): u is Admin => u.role === "admin";  // type GUARD ✔
let id: ID = "u_1";   // let n: number = "x";  // ✘ compile ERROR (not runtime surprise!)
Table 121 — The 80/20 type toolkit
ToolExampleUse
string/number/booleanlet n: numberHot-spot annotations

Unions`"light" \"dark"`Fixed choices (themes, roles, states!)
Literals`method: "GET" \"POST"`API contracts
unknown + narrowingif (typeof x === "string")SAFE any (validate outside data)

CODE  ·  Generics: one function, every type (10 minutes)
function first<T>(arr: T[]): T \| undefined { return arr[0]; }
first([1, 2]);        // T = number (inferred!)
first(["a"]);         // T = string
// Constraints keep power + safety:
function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T {
  return a.length >= b.length ? a : b;
}

interfacetype

1. npm i -D typescript; npx tsc --init (allowJs: true, checkJs: false)
2. Rename ONE hot file .js → .ts; fix ITS errors only
3. Enable strict gradually: strictNullChecks first (null bugs die!)
4. Type boundaries (API I/O with zod/valibot) before internals
Interview question — any vs unknown?

Expected: "any disables checking (contagious, banned except escape hatches). unknown forces narrowing before use — the safe way to type outside data like API responses and JSON.parse." Mention eslint @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any.

  server: { port: 5173, proxy: { "/api": "http://localhost:5000" } },  // dev: same-origin API ✔
  build: { outDir: "dist", sourcemap: true }

Realtime: SSE vs WebSockets

Table 126 — Push tech decision
NeedUseWhy
Server → browser stream (scores, progress, feeds)SSE (EventSource)HTTP-based, auto-reconnect, trivial
Two-way live (chat, games, collab)WebSockets (ws lib)Full-duplex, low latency
Rare updatesPolling (fetch every N s)Simple > clever at low frequency
CODE  ·  SSE in 15 lines (server + client)
// server: ordered stream over plain HTTP
app.get("/api/progress/:job", (req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "text/event-stream", "Cache-Control": "no-cache", Connection: "keep-alive" });
  const t = setInterval(() => res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify({ pct: pct() })}\n\n`), 500);
  req.on("close", () => clearInterval(t));
});
// client: auto-reconnecting stream
const es = new EventSource("/api/progress/7");
es.onmessage = e => paint(JSON.parse(e.data));
CODE  ·  WebSocket echo (npm i ws) — the two-way hello
import { WebSocketServer } from "ws";
const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 8080 });
wss.on("connection", ws => {
  ws.on("message", m => ws.send(`echo: ${m}`));   // broadcast: loop wss.clients!
});
Warning — Realtime honesty

Sockets add stateful servers (sticky sessions, horizontal-scale pain). Default to fetch/SSE; pay for WebSockets only when two-way + low-latency is the FEATURE (chat, games, live collab).

Exercise 55 — Live order tracker

SSE streams order status (received → cooking → on-way → delivered) with progress bar + auto-reconnect resume (Last-Event-ID) + graceful polling fallback if SSE blocked.

Solution

Server emits {stage, at} events with id: lines; client EventSource renders timeline; es.onerror → fetch-poll fallback. Same UX three ways — resilience engineering in miniature.

Relationships (say the sentence!)

SayModel (SQL)Model (Mongo)

CODE  ·  N-N done right (order_items join table)
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id INT REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id INT REFERENCES products(id),
  qty INT CHECK (qty > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

Normalize vs denormalize (the eternal trade)

Table 128 — The trade, honestly
Normalize (split, JOIN)Denormalize (duplicate, embed)
✔ One truth (update once)✔ Reads need zero JOINs (fast pages)
✔ No update anomalies✔ Matches read shapes (feeds, carts)
✘ JOINs on hot reads✘ Copies drift (sync/cron/eventual)
Rule: money/identity normalized; feeds/caches denormalizedSame rule, other side

Indexes + EXPLAIN (speed with proof)

CODE  ·  Index the WHERE/JOIN/ORDER paths (measure, don't guess!)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at DESC);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Seq Scan = table crawl (bad at scale!) ··· Index Scan = seek (good!)
Table 129 — Index wisdom
RuleWhy
Index FKs + WHERE + ORDER BY pathsJOINs/sorts/filters seek instead of crawl
Compound order matters (user, date)Serves user queries + user+date, NOT date-alone
Too many indexes = slow writesEach INSERT updates every index — index reads you HAVE
Partial/expression for hot slicesWHERE active partial, lower(email) unique (citext!)

Transactions + N+1

CODE  ·  Money moves atomically (all-or-nothing, concurrent-safe)
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 100;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;  -- or ROLLBACK on ANY failure (app code must!)
CODE  ·  N+1: 1 query + N follow-ups (the perf killer) → 1 JOIN instead
// ✘ 101 queries for 100 orders:
for (const o of orders) o.user = await User.findById(o.user_id);
// ✔ ONE query:
SELECT o.*, u.name FROM orders o JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id;
// Mongo: .populate() batches (2 queries, not N+1) ✔
Interview question — How do you find slow queries?

Expected: "EXPLAIN ANALYZE in staging with production-like data; log slow queries (log_min_duration_statement); fix with indexes/JOIN rewrites/pagination; re-measure. Never index blindly — every index taxes writes." Measurement-first = senior.

Exercise 56 — Model the book club

Books, members, loans (who-has-what + due), reviews. SQL schema + constraints + 3 indexes justified + 2 reports (overdue loans, top books) + loan/return as a transaction. EXPLAIN both reports.

Solution

loans(member FK, book FK, due, returned_at); UNIQUE active loan per book (partial index WHERE returned_at IS NULL!); reports via JOIN+GROUP; checkout = BEGIN … INSERT loan … UPDATE book stock … COMMIT. Constraints + partial indexes carry the integrity.

Table 131 — Router essentials
ToolJob

Context: shared state without drilling

CODE  ·  Theme + cart stores via Context (small-app state, zero libs)
import { createContext, useContext, useState, useMemo } from "react";
const CartCtx = createContext(null);
export const useCart = () => useContext(CartCtx);   // custom hook = clean API ✔
export function CartProvider({ children }) {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
  const value = useMemo(() => ({
    items,
    add: id => setItems(p => [...p, id]),
    count: items.length
  }), [items]);                                     // memo = no useless re-renders
  return <CartCtx.Provider value={value}>{children}</CartCtx.Provider>;
}
// App: <CartProvider><Router…/></CartProvider> ··· any child: const { count, add } = useCart();
Warning — Context ≠ state manager

Context broadcasts; it doesn't optimize. High-frequency updates (typing, drags) re-render ALL consumers. Split contexts (AuthCtx/CartCtx/ThemeCtx), memo values, and graduate to Zustand/Redux when updates fly.

Forms: controlled + validated + accessible

CODE  ·  The professional form pattern (state + errors + aria)
function Checkout() {
  const [form, setForm] = useState({ email: "", city: "" });
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});
  const set = k => e => setForm(f => ({ ...f, [k]: e.target.value }));
  const submit = e => {
    e.preventDefault();
    const errs = {};
    if (!/^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$/.test(form.email)) errs.email = "Valid email required";
    setErrors(errs);
    if (Object.keys(errs).length) return;
    placeOrder(form);
  };
  return (<form onSubmit={submit} noValidate>
    <label htmlFor="em">Email</label>
    <input id="em" value={form.email} onChange={set("email")} aria-invalid={!!errors.email} aria-describedby="em-err" />
    {errors.email && <p id="em-err" role="alert">{errors.email}</p>}
    <button>Pay</button>
  </form>);
}
Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Router owns URLS (shareable app state), Context owns SLOW shared state (auth/theme/cart), component state owns the rest (forms, toggles). Validate on submit + blur, announce with role=alert, and keep inputs controlled.

/cart (public) → /checkout (requires login: redirect with state.from) → /done (requires completed order). Persist cart to localStorage; restore on boot; clear after order. Deep-linking /checkout logged-out lands back post-login.

Solution

<RequireAuth><Checkout/></RequireAuth> wrapper (Navigate to /login state={{from}}); login navigates back to from||"/"; order context guards /done. Auth + router + persistence composed — the real SPA triangle.

Chapter 63

Interview Bank I — HTML & CSS (30 Questions)

All levels~ 120 min
Model answers for the HTML/CSS questions employers actually ask.
In this chapter
  • HTML semantics + forms + a11y (10)
  • CSS cascade/box/units (10)
  • Layout + responsive + motion (10)
  • How to answer (STAR + think-aloud)
InterviewCareer

Answering technique (read first!)

Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Structure EVERY answer: Claim (one sentence) → Explain (why/how) → Example (code or story) → Edge (gotcha + fix). "Specificity scores ID-class-element; an ID beats any classes; I keep selectors flat single-class; I debug in DevTools where losers are crossed out." 30 seconds, hired energy.

HTML (1–10)

Interview question — 1. Block vs inline?

Block (div/p/h1) takes full width and stacks; inline (span/a) flows in text and ignores width/height. inline-block flows inline AND accepts sizes. I center images with display:block + margin auto.

Interview question — 2. Semantic HTML — why bother?

Meaning for Google + screen readers + maintainability: header/nav/main/article/section/aside/footer form landmarks ("skip to content" works). Test: article = shareable alone; section = themed + heading; else div.

Interview question — 3. label + input done right?

<label for="id"> matches <input id> + name for submission; clicking focuses; readers announce. Placeholders are NOT labels. Groups use fieldset + legend.

Interview question — 4. How do you make images fast + accessible?

SVG icons, WebP/AVIF photos with picture fallbacks, width+height (CLS!), lazy below fold, hero fetchpriority high, descriptive alt (or alt="" decorative).

Interview question — 5. Local vs session storage vs cookies?

localStorage ~5MB forever (prefs); sessionStorage per-tab (wizards); cookies 4KB sent every request (auth via HttpOnly). Never secrets in localStorage (XSS-readable).

Interview question — 6. What is the viewport meta and why?

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> makes mobiles use real width — without it, responsive CSS never triggers and pages render tiny.

Interview question — 7. GET vs POST forms?

GET appends to URL (shareable, bookmarkable, length-limited, never secrets); POST hides in body (creates/updates, file uploads, CSRF-protected). Search = GET; register = POST.

Interview question — 8. How do you audit accessibility?

Keyboard-only run (Tab/Enter/focus visible), Lighthouse a11y 95+, contrast 4.5:1, labels/alt/landmarks, aria-current/labels, captions. Fix list before ship.

Interview question — 9. defer vs async scripts?

Both download in parallel; defer runs IN ORDER after parsing (default choice); async runs WHEN READY (orderless — analytics/ads). Neither blocks rendering like plain scripts.

Interview question — 10. How do you SEO a page?

Unique title + honest description, semantic headings, fast mobile-friendly (vitals!), descriptive alt/filenames, OG tags, canonical, sitemap + HTTPS. Content quality beats tricks.

CSS core (11–20)

Interview question — 11. Specificity battle — who wins?

Score ID-class-element left-to-right: #nav(1-0-0) beats .a.b.c(0-3-0). I write flat single classes so ORDER decides; !important only for utilities; DevTools shows losers crossed out.

Interview question — 12. content-box vs border-box?

content-box: width = content only (padding/border ADD → 344px surprise). border-box: width = total (sane). Universal ,::before,*::after{box-sizing:border-box} opens every stylesheet I write.

Interview question — 13. font-size vs font-weight?

Size = spatial scale (rem/px/vw); weight = stroke thickness (100–900). Big-light vs small-bold prove independence. rem type (user-scalable) + loaded real weights (no faux bold).

Interview question — 14. width vs max-width? height vs min-height?

Fixed width overflows phones → width:100% + max-width caps. Fixed height spills wrapped text → min-height elastic. Containers fluid, media aspect-ratio locked.

Interview question — 15. rem vs em vs px?

rem = root (type/spacing, accessible); em = parent-context (text-hugging padding); px = hairlines/borders. Body in rem respects browser font settings — legal-grade a11y.

Interview question — 16. Why is my margin not working? (collapsing!)

Vertical margins merge (max wins), parent/child merge through, empty elements collapse. Fixes: one-direction margins, parent padding, or gap in flex/grid (never collapses).

Interview question — 17. position absolute went to the page corner — why?

Absolute anchors to nearest POSITIONED ancestor; all-static parents → viewport root. Fix: position:relative on the intended parent. Bonus: fixed = viewport; sticky = threshold + scroll parent.

Interview question — 18. z-index ignored — debug steps?

z-index needs positioned/flex/grid items; then check stacking-context traps (parent opacity<1, transform, filter, z-index). Fix structure, not bigger numbers; use a --z-* scale.

Interview question — 19. line-height px vs unitless?

Unitless (1.6) multiplies each element's own size — headings/paragraphs both perfect. px inherits rigidly — 40px headings crushed into 24px lines. Unitless always.

Interview question — 20. How do you theme light/dark?

CSS variables for ALL colors + [data-theme="dark"] overrides + JS toggle persisted to localStorage + prefers-color-scheme default. No hardcoded colors anywhere (the toggle test finds them).

Layout + responsive + motion (21–30)

Interview question — 21. Flexbox vs Grid?

Flexbox = 1D (row OR column): navs, rows, centering. Grid = 2D (rows AND columns): scaffolding, galleries. Compose: grid page + flex components. justify=main/row axis, align=cross/column.

Interview question — 22. Center a div — all the ways?

Flex (justify+align center), grid (place-items center), absolute (50% + translate(-50%,-50%)), margin auto (known width), text-align (inline). Modern default: flex/grid one-liners.

Interview question — 23. Explain repeat(auto-fit, minmax(260px, 1fr)).

"As many ≥260px tracks as fit; stretch to share leftovers; drop columns as space shrinks." Responsive galleries, zero media queries. auto-fit collapses empties (vs auto-fill).

Interview question — 24. Mobile-first workflow?

Base CSS = phone; min-width layers enhance upward. Breakpoints from CONTENT pain (resize till ugly), not devices. One codebase, fast core for all.

Interview question — 25. clamp() for fluid type?

clamp(MIN, fluid-vw, MAX): floor + growth + ceiling. h1 clamp(1.75rem, 1rem+4vw, 3.5rem) scales smoothly with zero breakpoints and never explodes.

Interview question — 26. 60fps animation rule?

Animate transform + opacity ONLY (GPU compositor). width/top/margin trigger layout+paint per frame (jank). translate instead of top; scale instead of width. Plus prefers-reduced-motion fallback.

Interview question — 27. Responsive images strategy?

picture + WebP/AVIF sources + img fallback, srcset/sizes, lazy below fold, hero preload + fetchpriority, width/height anti-CLS. Art direction via media sources.

Interview question — 28. BEM — sell it in 20 seconds?

Block__Element--Modifier: flat single classes → zero specificity wars, readable HTML, greppable, scales to 10k lines. .card__price--sale tells everything.

Interview question — 29. Page has horizontal scroll on mobile — fix?

Find overflow (DevTools, scroll the tree): fixed widths → max-width; long words → overflow-wrap; wide tables → scroll wrapper; negative margins; 100vw + scrollbar. Test 360px.

Interview question — 30. How do you organize a big stylesheet?

Tokens (variables) → reset → base/typography → layout → components (BEM) → utilities; or layers (@layer reset,base,components,utilities). One pattern, enforced by lint.

Chapter 64

Interview Bank II — JavaScript (35 Questions)

All levels~ 150 min
The JS questions that decide offers: scope, async, DOM and architecture.
In this chapter
  • Language core (12)
  • Functions/scope/this (8)
  • Async + APIs (8)
  • DOM + browser (7)
InterviewCareer

Language core (1–12)

Interview question — 1. let vs const vs var?

const default (binding locked), let for reassignment, var retired (function scope + silent redeclare + undefined hoisting). Block scope + TDZ for both modern ones.

Interview question — 2. Primitives vs references?

Primitives copy VALUES (independent); objects copy POINTERS (shared). const locks binding, not contents. Spread = shallow; structuredClone = deep.

Interview question — 3. == vs ===?

=== always (type + value). == coerces (0=="0", ""==0 chaos). Falsy eight: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN.

Interview question — 4. || vs ?? vs ?. ?

|| falls back on ANY falsy (kills 0/""); ?? only null/undefined (safe defaults); ?. dives safely (undefined, no crash). Combo: user?.city ?? "Unknown".

Interview question — 5. for...of vs for...in?

of = iterable VALUES (arrays ✔); in = object KEYS (+ inherited! never for arrays). Classic for = index control; while = unknown iterations.

Interview question — 6. map vs forEach?

map BUILDS a new array (same length, chainable); forEach DOES effects (returns undefined). Building with forEach+push is junior style.

Interview question — 7. reduce in one breath?

Combines all into one: reduce((acc,x)=>…, INIT). Always pass INIT (empty arrays throw without). Totals, groups, histograms.

Interview question — 8. sort() surprise?

Default is ALPHABETIC ([10,9,80]→[10,80,9]!) and IN-PLACE. Numbers need (a,b)=>a-b; copy first ([...a].sort / toSorted) unless mutation intended.

Interview question — 9. Destructuring + spread depth?

Unpack/merge in one gesture — but SHALLOW (nested shared). Deep = structuredClone. Rest collects (...args); spread expands f(...arr).

Interview question — 10. Template literals — why default?

${} injection + multiline + tagged templates (safe SQL/HTML builders) beat concatenation in readability and safety.

Interview question — 11. Map vs Object? Set superpower?

Map: any keys + size + order + no prototype traps (dictionaries). Set: auto-unique + O(1) has (dedupe: [...new Set(a)]). Objects: records + JSON.

Interview question — 12. Shallow vs deep copy — full answer?

Spread/slice top-level only (nested shared — the trap). structuredClone deep (no functions/DOM). JSON trick legacy (loses Dates/functions). Never mutate unowned inputs.

Functions/scope/this (13–20)

Interview question — 13. What is a closure? Real use?

Function + captured lexical scope = remembers birthplace vars after outer returns. Uses: private state (counters/vaults), factories, handlers remembering data. Demo createCounter on request.

Interview question — 14. this in 30 seconds?

HOW called: obj.m()→obj; f()→undefined; new→instance; call/apply/bind→forced; arrows→inherit enclosing (no own this). Arrows for callbacks, methods for objects.

Interview question — 15. Arrow vs function?

Arrows: short + lexical this + no arguments/prototype (not constructible). Functions: own this + hoisted declarations. Callbacks→arrows; methods/constructors→function/class.

Interview question — 16. Hoisting truth?

function declarations hoist WHOLE (callable early); var hoists undefined (bug factory); let/const sit in TDZ (ReferenceError before line). Write declarations top-down anyway.

Interview question — 17. Debounce vs throttle?

Debounce: run AFTER quiet (search input). Throttle: run at STEADY rate (scroll/resize). Both cap storms; debounce waits, throttle paces.

Interview question — 18. Pure functions — why?

Same input→same output, no side effects = testable, cacheable, parallelizable. Impure (random/date/mutate) isolated at edges. map/filter/reduce love purity.

Interview question — 19. Rest vs spread vs arguments?

...args gathers (rest, real array, modern); f(...a) expands (spread); arguments is legacy array-like (no map, banned in arrows — use rest).

Interview question — 20. IIFE / modules for privacy?

Old: IIFE ((()=>{…})()) hides scope. Modern: ESM (export only the API) + closures. Modules evaluate once = singleton by default.

Async + APIs (21–28)

Interview question — 21. Event loop in 45 seconds?

Sync runs on stack; microtasks (promises) drain FULLY; render; ONE macrotask (timeout/IO); repeat. Promise.then beats setTimeout(…,0) always. Blocking sync starves render.

Interview question — 22. Promise states + combinators?

pending→fulfilled/rejected (settled once). all (need all, fail-fast), allSettled (partial OK), race (first finish), any (first success). Parallel independent work with all.

Interview question — 23. fetch gotchas?

Resolves on 404/500 (check res.ok!), rejects only network-down. Needs timeout (AbortSignal), JSON try/catch, auth headers, 4 UI states (loading/empty/error/ready).

Interview question — 24. async/await rules?

await in async only; every await can throw → try/catch/finally; parallel via Promise.all (not sequential loops); always timeout network; rethrow or handle (no silent catch{}).

Interview question — 25. How do you handle API errors in UI?

State machine: loading skeleton → empty / error+retry / ready. Never blank screens; toasts for mutations; optimistic UI with rollback for speed + honesty.

Interview question — 26. Callback hell → modern chain?

Nested callbacks → promise chains (.then) → async/await (sync-looking). Errors bubble to one catch; finally cleans up. Flat > nested, always.

Interview question — 27. AbortController — why?

Cancels in-flight fetch + abortable listeners + timeouts (AbortSignal.timeout). Prevents race conditions (old search overwriting new) and leaks on unmount.

Interview question — 28. Microtask starvation?

Infinite promise chains (recursive .then) block render/macrotasks forever — frozen UI with "working" code. Fix: yield to macrotasks (setTimeout/rAF chunks) for huge jobs.

DOM + browser (29–35)

Interview question — 29. textContent vs innerHTML?

textContent = safe TEXT (user data ✔); innerHTML parses HTML (XSS with untrusted input!). Build user content via createElement/textContent; innerHTML only for own static templates.

Interview question — 30. Event delegation — sell it?

One parent listener + e.target.closest() handles infinite/dynamic children: constant memory, zero re-binding, new rows free. Bubbling is the mechanism; closest finds the actor.

Interview question — 31. target vs currentTarget?

target = deepest clicked element; currentTarget = listener's element. Delegation lives on their difference (button vs list). Mixing them breaks handlers.

Interview question — 32. Efficient big-list rendering?

DocumentFragment batch (one reflow), innerHTML-once for trusted templates, virtualize 10k+ rows, content-visibility:auto, passive scroll listeners, rAF writes.

Interview question — 33. FormData + validation combo?

new FormData(form) reads all named controls; Constraint API (checkValidity/reportValidity/setCustomValidity) for UX; server revalidates everything (browser checks are bypassable).

Interview question — 34. localStorage corrupted — app must survive?

JSON.parse in try/catch with defaults (load(k, fallback)); schema-check shapes; version keys (v1:) for migrations. Boot never crashes on bad data.

Interview question — 35. XSS in 30 seconds?

Attacker JS via unsafe sinks (innerHTML/location/eval). Defenses: textContent/createElement, escape + sanitize, CSP headers, HttpOnly cookies. Stored > reflected > DOM flavors.

Interview Bank III — Backend, DB, Auth & React (25 Questions)

All levels~ 120 min

In this chapter

InterviewCareer

Node/Express/REST (1–8)

Interview question — 1. Node event loop — why single-threaded scales?

One thread takes requests; libuv pool does I/O async; callbacks resume. Thousands concurrent, zero thread overhead. Rule: NEVER block (no sync I/O/crypto in handlers).

Interview question — 2. Design POST /orders (REST)?

Noun URL + version (/api/v1/orders), validate body → 400 {errors}, create → 201 + resource, auth → 401/403, errors one shape {error:{message}}, idempotency key for retries.

Interview question — 3. Middleware order matters — prove it?

cors → json → logger → auth → routes → 404 → error-last. json after routes = body undefined; error handler not last = crashes escape; auth placement scopes protection.

Interview question — 4. Central error handling?

next(err) → 4-arg middleware (last!): log full, send {status, generic-or-known message}, never stacks to clients, separate 4xx (client) vs 5xx (bugs + alerts).

Interview question — 5. Pagination that scales?

limit/offset + caps (max 100) + meta {page,pages,total}; deep pages → keyset (WHERE id > last, ORDER BY id LIMIT n). Never unbounded lists.

Interview question — 6. File uploads safely?

Size caps, mime+extension allowlist, uuid renames (path traversal!), outside webroot/object storage, image re-encode (strip metadata), async scan. Serve with safe Content-Type.

Interview question — 7. CORS error — what's happening?

Browser blocks cross-origin reads without server permission. Fix SERVER-side: exact origins (never * with credentials), methods/headers allowlist, preflight handling. Dev: Vite proxy.

Interview question — 8. How do you structure an Express app?

routes (validate+call) → services (logic) → data layer (DB); middleware (auth/errors/log); config from env; versioned paths; tests per layer. Thin routes, fat services.

SQL/NoSQL/modeling (9–14)

Interview question — 9. SQL vs NoSQL — decide like a senior?

Money/relations/reports → SQL (ACID+JOINs+constraints). Flexible/reads/shapeshift → NoSQL (embed read-together). Split per bounded context, not per company. Both is normal.

Interview question — 10. INNER vs LEFT JOIN?

INNER = matched pairs only; LEFT = all left + NULLs (find inactive users!). Draw the Venn; default to LEFT for reports including zeros.

Interview question — 11. N+1 and the fix?

1 query + N follow-ups (loop-fetching relations) = latency death. Fix: JOIN (SQL) / populate+lean (Mongo) / dataloaders (GraphQL). Prove with query logs before/after.

Interview question — 12. Embed vs reference in Mongo?

Embed: read-together + bounded (post+comments). Reference: independent/unbounded/shared (users, products). Overflow pattern for grown arrays (latest N + count).

Interview question — 13. Transactions — when?

Multi-write integrity (transfer, checkout): BEGIN…COMMIT, ROLLBACK on any failure, balance checks INSIDE the txn (race-safe). Money without txns = eventually wrong.

Interview question — 14. Index strategy in 30 seconds?

Index WHERE/JOIN/ORDER paths (compound order matters!), EXPLAIN ANALYZE to prove, partial/expression for hot slices. Every index taxes writes — index reads you HAVE.

Auth/security (15–20)

Interview question — 15. bcrypt — why and how?

Adaptive one-way hash + auto-salt; cost 12 (~250ms); compare() timing-safe. Same 401 message either way (no user enumeration). Never plain/MD5/SHA-direct.

Interview question — 16. Sessions vs JWT?

Sessions: server store + instant revoke (monoliths). JWT: stateless verify + short access + rotating refresh in HttpOnly cookie (APIs/mobile). Payload is PUBLIC (signed, not secret).

Interview question — 17. Where do tokens live?

Access in memory, refresh in HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookie. Never localStorage (XSS steals all). Short expiry + rotation + versioned global logout.

Interview question — 18. Top 3 vulnerabilities + fixes?

Injection (parameterize + validate), XSS (safe render + CSP + HttpOnly), broken auth (bcrypt + short tokens + rate limits). Then CSRF (SameSite+tokens) + headers/rate hygiene.

Interview question — 19. CSRF defense stack?

SameSite cookies (primary) + per-form tokens + custom-header/API preflight + GET-never-mutates. Explain the evil.com-auto-posting-to-bank.com story.

Interview question — 20. Rate limiting — where and how?

Auth routes strict (20/15min), APIs generous (300/15min), 429 + Retry-After, keyed by IP+user, Redis store in prod. Brute-force dies here.

React (21–25)

Interview question — 21. Props vs state?

Props flow DOWN read-only (parent owns); state is owned + setState re-renders. Lift shared state to lowest common parent; derive (totals) instead of storing.

Interview question — 22. Why keys? Why not index?

Keys = stable identity across renders (preserve state/focus, minimal DOM ops). Index breaks on reorder/filter (wrong state attached). Use ids, always.

Interview question — 23. useEffect deps array?

[] once; [x] on change; missing = stale closures; absent = every render (loop risk). Cleanup (abort/unsubscribe) prevents leaks + StrictMode double-runs.

Interview question — 24. Controlled vs uncontrolled?

Controlled: value+onChange in state (validate/disable/instant UX — default). Uncontrolled: refs read on demand (simple one-shots, file inputs, focus).

Interview question — 25. Mutating state directly — what breaks?

Same reference = React skips render (silent stale UI). Always new objects ([...p], filter, map). Immutability enables cheap change detection + time-travel.

Exercise 64 — C1 (2). groupBy(items, keyFn)

Return {key: [items]}. Empty-safe.

Solution

const groupBy=(a,f)=>a.reduce((o,x)=>{const k=f(x);(o[k]??=[]).push(x);return o},{}) — init {} handles empty ✔.

Exercise 65 — C2 (2). debounce(fn, ms)

Trailing-edge with cancel().

Solution

const debounce=(f,ms)=>{let t;const w=(...a)=>{clearTimeout(t);t=setTimeout(()=>f(...a),ms)};w.cancel=()=>clearTimeout(t);return w}.

Exercise 66 — C3 (3). fetchJson(url, {timeout, retries})

ok-check + timeout + 1 retry on 5xx/network + typed error.

Solution

Loop attempts: AbortSignal.timeout; !ok → throw status (retry iff ≥500); network throws → retry once; final throw Error(GET ${url}: ${msg}). Always 4-state UI around it.

async function fetchJson(url, { timeout = 8000, retries = 1, ...opts } = {}) {
  for (let i = 0; i <= retries; i++) {
    try {
      const r = await fetch(url, { ...opts, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeout) });
      if (!r.ok) { if (r.status < 500 || i === retries) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status}`); continue; }
      return await r.json();
    } catch (e) { if (i === retries) throw e; }
  }
}

const throttle = (f, ms = 200) => { let last = 0; return (...a) => { const n = Date.now(); if (n - last >= ms) { last = n; f(...a); } }; };

function useFetch(url) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ status: "loading" });
  useEffect(() => { const c = new AbortController();
    (async () => { try { const r = await fetch(url, { signal: c.signal });
      if (!r.ok) throw new Error(r.status); const data = await r.json();
      setState({ status: data.length ? "ready" : "empty", data }); }
    catch (e) { if (e.name !== "AbortError") setState({ status: "error", error: e }); } })();
    return () => c.abort(); }, [url]);
  return state;
}

r.get("/", asyncH(async (req, res) => {
  const { q = "", author = "", after = "", limit = 20 } = req.query;
  let rows = await store.all("books");
  if (q) rows = rows.filter(b => (b.title + b.author).toLowerCase().includes(q.toLowerCase()));
  if (author) rows = rows.filter(b => b.author === author);
  rows.sort((a, b) => a.id.localeCompare(b.id));
  const i = after ? rows.findIndex(b => b.id === after) + 1 : 0;
  const data = rows.slice(i, i + Math.min(+limit, 50));
  res.json({ data, next: data.length ? data[data.length - 1].id : null });
}));
CODE  ·  63. Paginated list component (React + keyset "Load more")
function Books() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([]); const [next, setNext] = useState(null);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState("loading");
  const load = async (after = "") => {
    setStatus("loading");
    try {
      const r = await fetch(`/api/v1/books?after=${after}&limit=20`).then(x => x.json());
      setItems(p => after ? [...p, ...r.data] : r.data); setNext(r.next); setStatus("ready");
    } catch { setStatus("error"); }
  };
  useEffect(() => { load(); }, []);
  if (status === "loading" && !items.length) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (status === "error") return <p role="alert">Failed. <button onClick={() => load()}>Retry</button></p>;
  return (<><ul>{items.map(b => <li key={b.id}>{b.title}</li>)}</ul>
    {next && <button onClick={() => load(next)}>Load more</button>}</>);
}

// /health = alive ··· /ready = can serve (DB ok?) — orchestrators NEED both
app.get("/health", (req, res) => res.json({ ok: true }));
app.get("/ready", asyncH(async (req, res) => {
  await pool.query("SELECT 1");
  res.json({ ok: true, db: "up", uptime: process.uptime() });
}));
CODE  ·  69. CSV export (stream 1M rows, memory flat)
// GET /api/v1/orders.csv — stream, never build the string!
app.get("/api/v1/orders.csv", requireAuth, asyncH(async (req, res) => {
  res.set({ "Content-Type": "text/csv", "Content-Disposition": "attachment; filename=orders.csv" });
  res.write("id,total,created\n");
  for await (const o of orderStream(req.userId)) res.write(`${o.id},${o.total},${o.created}\n`);
  res.end();
}));
CODE  ·  70. Nightly purge (cron + idempotent handler)
// cron: 0 3 * * * node src/jobs/purge.js — delete soft-deleted >30d, in batches
import { store } from "../store.js";
const cutoff = Date.now() - 30 * 864e5;
for (const c of ["notes", "reviews"]) {
  const rows = await store.all(c);
  const victims = rows.filter(r => r.deletedAt && Date.parse(r.deletedAt) < cutoff);
  for (const v of victims) await store.remove(c, x => x.id === v.id);
  console.log(`purged ${victims.length} from ${c}`);
}
CODE  ·  71. OAuth login sketch (GitHub, 20 lines of concepts)
// 1. Link: https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=..&scope=read:user
// 2. GitHub → GET /auth/github?code=.. — exchange code for token (server-to-server!)
// 3. Fetch profile with token → find-or-create user → issue YOUR jwt (same as login!)
// NEVER trust profile email blindly: verify + link to existing accounts carefully.
app.get("/auth/github", asyncH(async (req, res) => {
  const t = await exchangeCode(req.query.code);          // POST github.com/login/oauth/access_token
  const gh = await fetch("https://api.github.com/user", { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${t}` } }).then(r => r.json());
  const user = await findOrCreateByGithub(gh);
  res.json({ access: jwt.sign({ sub: user.id }, SECRET, { expiresIn: "15m" }), user });
}));
CODE  ·  72. Sitemap + robots (SEO discovery, generated)
// GET /sitemap.xml — build from DB (cache 1h!); robots.txt points at it
app.get("/sitemap.xml", asyncH(async (req, res) => {
  const books = await store.all("books");
  res.type("xml").send(`<?xml version="1.0"?><urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">` +
    books.map(b => `<url><loc>https://bookhub.dev/books/${b.id}</loc></url>`).join("") + `</urlset>`);
}));
// public/robots.txt:  User-agent: *\nAllow: /\nSitemap: https://bookhub.dev/sitemap.xml

CODE  ·  Proposal anatomy (wins against 50 bids)
1. First line: THEIR problem restated ("Your menu PDF loses mobile orders…")
2. Plan: 3 milestones with dates (shows you scoped it!)
3. Proof: ONE similar build + metric ("…+38% calls in 60 days")
4. Price + timeline + what-you-need-from-them (decisive, easy yes)

Key takeaway — Key takeaway

Income = proof × visibility × trust. Proof: 3 shipped builds with metrics. Visibility: portfolio + GitHub green + LinkedIn posts (build in public!). Trust: fast replies, scoped promises, delivered demos. Do all three for 90 days — opportunities compound.

Exercise 75 — The 90-day earn plan

Days 1–30: finish capstone + portfolio + 3 READMEs + LinkedIn (post weekly builds). Days 31–60: 5 tailored proposals/week + 2 mock interviews/week + contribute 1 OSS fix. Days 61–90: close first gig OR 10 real interviews; log every no + lesson. Review weekly; adjust, never stop.

Solution

Success metric: not "a job by day 90" but "10 real conversations + 1 paid gig or final-round". Conversations compound into offers. The log (proposals sent, replies, lessons) IS the system — systems beat motivation.
